README.md.overview: The front door of chat-analyzer-pro and the anchor of tour Step 1: a Python 3.11+ CLI that turns a WhatsApp .txt, Telegram .json, or .zip chat export into terminal insights plus a single self-contained offline HTML report — one command, entirely on your machine. It introduces the project's central design idea (an always-on feature tier vs. the optional [nlp] extra), the quickstart that replays the bundled sample chats, the privacy guarantees, and the environment-variable configuration table that the rest of the tour builds on.

sections.title: Title and one-line pitch
sections.explanation: The document opens with the essential promise: v0.1.0 converts WhatsApp `.txt`, Telegram `.json`, or `.zip` exports into terminal insights plus one self-contained HTML report with a single command. Three guarantees are compressed into the tagline — no accounts, no uploads, no telemetry — which is the privacy stance every later section assumes. The Python >= 3.11 floor is also stated up front, matching `requires-python` in pyproject.toml. The leading HTML comment records that the file is generated by the project's doc-writer tooling.

sections.title: Features: always-on vs NLP-gated
sections.explanation: This is the two-tier feature story the whole architecture is built around. The base install (lines 9–18) lists what every user gets with no model download: message stats, top words/emojis, VADER sentiment, relationship health with a gamified friendship index, a directed interaction network with a drag-to-rotate 3D ECharts view, and the Tier A heuristic narrative that is always labelled speculative. Lines 20–24 add the gated tier: six-class emotion classification and the Tier B generative paragraph, where flan-T5 deliberately reads an ASCII digest of derived statistics — never raw chat text. Line 18 also explains why the report stays portable: ECharts and echarts-gl are vendored and inlined, so one HTML file works offline.

sections.title: Quickstart with bundled samples
sections.explanation: The four-step quickstart covers exporting a chat from WhatsApp and Telegram Desktop, then installing with `pip install -e .` in a virtualenv. Step 3 is the key demo path: `chat-analyzer data/sample_chats/whatsapp_sample.txt` runs the bundled sample, so you can try the tool before you ever export your own chat — this same sample reappears as a tour node in Step 5 and as a golden-test fixture in Step 12. Line 48 pins the CLI behavior contract: no arguments re-prompts interactively, `--version`/`--help` work, `python -m chat_analyzer` is equivalent to the console script, success exits 0, and failures exit 1 with a friendly message — never a traceback.

sections.title: Input format matrix
sections.explanation: A compact table maps each file extension to what the tool recognizes: `.txt` as a WhatsApp export, `.json` as a Telegram Desktop export, and `.zip` as a full archive whose transcripts are listed for the user to pick from (merged when several are selected). The 'counted honestly, never silently dropped' note for .txt previews the honest skip-counting design you will see in the parsers. Lines 60–61 pin two user-visible details: the report filename is derived from the input stem with sanitization and always written to the current working directory, and browser auto-open is best-effort with the `CHAT_ANALYZER_NO_OPEN=1` opt-out.

sections.title: NLP tiers and model sizes
sections.explanation: This section defines the 3-option tier menu that cli/main.py renders on every interactive run: tier 1 without NLP (default), tier 2 Minimal (~0.6 GB CPU-only torch), and tier 3 Full-fledged (~3 GB full torch). The two Hugging Face models are named with sizes — distilbert-base-uncased-emotion (~255 MB) and flan-t5-small (~340 MB) — and are downloaded once into the local HF cache. The announce-before-download rule appears here too: names and sizes are printed before any install starts, and any failure degrades to basic analysis instead of freezing. Lines 79–81 cover the non-interactive path (`CHAT_ANALYZER_TIER` beating the legacy `CHAT_ANALYZER_FORCE_NLP`) and the Windows MAX_PATH guard with its `scripts/make_nlp_env.ps1` workaround — the subject of tour Step 9.

sections.title: Large chats and performance
sections.explanation: Three mechanisms keep huge exports tractable, and each maps to a code area later in the tour: deterministic stratified sampling above `CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_SAMPLE` (50,000 by default, `random_state=42` so results are reproducible and explicitly labelled as sample-based), parallel exact scoring via a process pool above 20,000 unique texts with truncation-safe batches and a partial-rescue fallback, and strictly opt-in INT8 quantization (off by default because it distorts scores). The performance table is a measured snapshot from `scripts/benchmark.py` on a 424,826-message export: 64.3 s full pipeline vs a 243.7 s baseline, zero `strptime()` calls per parse — a headline number justified by the fast-path datetime parsing you will read in whatsapp_parser.py. The caveat about thermal throttling explains why cross-session timings spread ±40%.

sections.title: Privacy and honest reporting
sections.explanation: Five bullets formalize the privacy stance: everything runs locally with no uploads or telemetry; the opt-in result cache stores derived scalars only, never raw chat text; report filenames are sanitized and chat content is treated as untrusted input (Jinja2 autoescaping is on); both narrative tiers always carry speculative disclaimers; and sampled emotion results are labelled while skipped/system lines are counted instead of silently dropped. Each bullet corresponds to a concrete implementation you will encounter — result_cache.py, report_html.py's autoescape, the narrative modules, and the parsers' honest counters.

sections.title: Environment-variable configuration
sections.explanation: The full knob table: `CHAT_ANALYZER_TIER` (non-interactive tier override, wins over the legacy flag), `CHAT_ANALYZER_FORCE_NLP` (0→tier 1, 1→tier 3), `CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_SAMPLE`, `CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_WORKERS`, `CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_QUANT` (opt-in INT8), `CHAT_ANALYZER_RESULT_CACHE` (off by default), `CHAT_ANALYZER_NO_OPEN`, and `CHAT_ANALYZER_ALLOW_LONG_PATH`. Every one is optional, and the main.py/pipeline.py code resolves exactly these names. The result-cache detail block explains the key recipe — SHA-256 of the file bytes plus a config signature including schema version, app version, NLP state, sample cap, worker count, and chosen zip transcripts — plus storage outside the repo, atomic writes, 30-day pruning, and the guarantee that the HTML report is regenerated fresh even on a cache hit.

sections.title: Development, docs, and license
sections.explanation: The development block shows the three commands every contributor runs: editable install with the `[dev]` extra, `ruff check src tests`, and pytest (with `-m "not slow"` for the fast subset — the `slow` marker is declared in pyproject.toml). The documentation links map each docs file to its purpose, including ARCHITECTURE.md which is tour Step 2. The license section is deliberately candid: no license is declared as of v0.1.0, while the vendored ECharts assets ship under their own Apache 2.0 and BSD 3-Clause files. The trailing VERIFY comment is an open TODO flagging that licensing must be settled before publishing.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.overview: The project's map, read as tour Step 2 before any code: an ASCII pipeline diagram (parsers → ingest → sample decision → result cache → always-on analysis → [nlp] gate → adapter → reporting outputs), a complete inventory of every src/chat_analyzer module, and the data contract boundary that separates the layers. It also records the key design decisions — CLI-first Typer, lazy heavy imports, the [nlp] gate, Option C sampling, the opt-in result cache, and the single-file HTML report. Every later tour step fills in one block of this diagram, so keep it in mind while reading the code.

sections.title: Header and system overview
sections.explanation: The header pins what is documented: version 0.1.0, the `chat-analyzer-pro` package in a src/ layout, and the Python >= 3.11 runtime. The overview prose states the core UX contract: a single command (`chat-analyzer <chat_file>`) with no `analyze` subcommand — the command is collapsed into the app root — where a positional path runs analysis directly, no argument runs an interactive re-prompt loop, and `--version`/`--help` remain available. This single-command design is a deliberate decision (D-02) you will see implemented verbatim in cli/main.py.

sections.title: ASCII pipeline diagram
sections.explanation: This is the map the whole tour walks. Read it top-down: raw chat export → PARSERS (WhatsAppParser .txt, telegram_parser .json) which return `(rows, counts)` as plain dicts — never a DataFrame — then the ParseReport dataclass boundary → INGEST, where `messages_to_dataframe()` builds the canonical tz-naive UTC DataFrame → the Option C sample decision (only when NLP is on) → the opt-in result cache keyed by file hash plus config → the ALWAYS-ON ANALYSIS block (ChatEDA, VADER sentiment, relationship health, network, matplotlib figures, Tier A narrative) → the fork where the [nlp] gate is OFF (emotion stays None, report renders an 'unavailable' note) or ON (EmotionAnalyzer + Tier B flan-T5 narrative) → the ADAPTER that squeezes everything into the AnalysisResults TypedDict → final outputs: the terminal summary, the regenerated-every-time HTML report, and the best-effort browser open. Each box later becomes a tour step.

sections.title: Zip behavior and module inventory
sections.explanation: The zip paragraph clarifies the trickiest input: a `.zip` may hold multiple transcripts, `cli/zip_input.py` lets the user pick which to analyze and merges rows + counts into one ParseReport, and `parse_zip_with_report()` returns a 4-tuple whose `chosen_names` rides in the result-cache key — so picking different transcripts on the same zip invalidates the cache by construction. The module inventory table then lists every module with one-line responsibilities, which is the fastest way to see the layering: cli/ owns orchestration and contracts, parser/ and ingest/ own format handling, analysis/ owns computation, utils/ owns text/chart helpers, and reporting/ holds the PDF and weekly-digest modules that ship but are explicitly NOT wired into the CLI (deferred to v2).

sections.title: Data flow and message schema
sections.explanation: This section defines the three data contracts the pipeline speaks. First, the parser boundary: every parser returns `(rows: list[dict], counts: dict)` where counts carries total_lines, parsed_messages, skipped_lines, and system_messages — the 'honest counters' the README promised. Second, the parser-level row shape (shown as a code block for WhatsApp) with an un-fabricated datetime, sender, message, message_length, and derived date/time/hour fields; Telegram rows add message_id and normalize to naive UTC. Third, the canonical DataFrame from `messages_to_dataframe()` — the ONLY dict→df builder — whose columns are datetime, timestamp (an alias the chart visualizer requires), date, hour, sender, message, message_length, source, and uid. Finally the report contract table enumerates every AnalysisResults key, including the notable rules that `emotion` is None (never a crash) when the gate is OFF, and `report_path` is forced to `""` on a cache load so the HTML is always regenerated.

sections.title: CLI-first and lazy imports
sections.explanation: Two foundational decisions. CLI-first: the previous Streamlit app and its runtime `exec()` of downloaded modules were deleted entirely — the package ships only the typer CLI, there is no web server, no unsafe HTML, and no remote code fetch; failures always end in `typer.Exit(code=1) from None`, never a traceback, and `--version` is implemented as an eager callback because typer 0.27 lacks a built-in flag. Lazy heavy imports: only typer plus stdlib are imported at module level so `--help`/`--version` stay instant; the analysis modules and matplotlib are imported inside `run_pipeline`/`_analyze_path`, and `matplotlib.use("Agg")` anchors the non-interactive backend before any pyplot import — the order matters on headless machines.

sections.title: The [nlp] gate
sections.explanation: The base install must never pull torch/transformers — they live only behind the optional `[nlp]` extra (torch>=2.0, transformers>=4.30,<5.15, sentencepiece>=0.1.99). The gate is a silent availability probe: `nlp_gate.nlp_available(MODEL_ID)` just tries importing torch and transformers and never raises or prompts. Tier resolution happens in main(): tier 2/3 resolve `nlp_status()` (READY / OUTDATED / MISSING), and MISSING triggers `install_nlp(cpu_only)` + `download_models()` so weights are cached before the pipeline's first use, OUTDATED offers 'Update now / Go with current', and the model name + size are always announced before any `from_pretrained` (the D-05 rule). Gated stages degrade, never crash: EmotionAnalyzer falls back to a rule-based classifier when the model load fails, and the Tier B narrative falls back to Tier A. The Windows MAX_PATH guard (WinError 206 with torch wheels) warns before multi-GB downloads and points to scripts/make_nlp_env.ps1, with `CHAT_ANALYZER_ALLOW_LONG_PATH=1` as the override.

sections.title: Option C sampling and parallel scoring
sections.explanation: The emotion stage scales two ways, and both knobs live in nlp_gate/analysis/emotion.py rather than the CLI. Sampled path (Option C): above the `CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_SAMPLE` cap (default 50,000; 0/off disables sampling) a tty prompt asks (default NO = exact) while piped/CI runs auto-sample; the sample itself is deterministic and (participant, time)-stratified with `random_state=42`, the frame gains an `emotion_scored` column plus `df.attrs["emotion_sample"]` metadata, and every output labels 'based on a sample of N of M messages'. Parallel exact scoring: unique texts are deduplicated (emotion is a pure function of text), and above 20,000 unique texts with `CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_WORKERS` ≥ 2 a ProcessPoolExecutor maps fixed-order chunks through a module-level, spawn-safe `_score_text_chunk` — JSON-able args only, the pipeline is built inside each child, torch threads are clamped, and chunks merge as they complete so results stay byte-identical to sequential. Failure is a partial rescue: completed chunk scores are kept and only lost chunks are re-scored sequentially. The Aug-2026 perf pass adds truncation-safe batching (a 512-character emoji-dense message can still exceed the 512-token limit), bounded chunk counts for load balancing, vectorized column write-back, and opt-in INT8 quantization (~1.7× faster but ~75% dominant-label agreement, applied identically in parent and children). Quarterly aggregation closes the section: per-quarter means feed the emotion-quarterly ECharts timeline.

sections.title: Result cache and Tier A/B narrative
sections.explanation: The opt-in result cache (default OFF) turns repeat runs into seconds: the key is sha256 of the raw file bytes folded with a config signature (schema, app_version, nlp_on, sample_cap, emotion_workers, chosen_transcripts), so any file edit, tier change, or zip-pick change invalidates it by construction. Storage lives outside the repo as a privacy lock, payload is derived data only, writes are atomic with a 30-day TTL prune, load is json-only with self-healing of corrupt files, and `report_path` is forced empty so the HTML is always regenerated. The narrative split then defines the two tiers: Tier A (always on, pandas + re only) produces hedged observations from conservative confidence thresholds; Tier B (gate ON only) summarizes a compact ASCII digest built from the Tier A observations — never raw chat text — via flan-t5-small, and any failure keeps the Tier A output so the run never crashes.

sections.title: HTML report, contracts, console hardening
sections.explanation: Three contract-heavy subsections. The single-file HTML report: an inline Jinja2 template with autoescape explicitly enabled because chat content is untrusted, vendored echarts/echarts-gl bundles inlined via importlib.resources (no CDN, works offline), interactive ECharts specs injected via `|tojson` with PNG data URIs as the validated fallback, per-chart failure isolation (`_safe_chart`), sanitized filenames, explicit UTF-8 writes, and best-effort browser open. The contract boundary rules: core modules never import CLI contracts, `adapters.adapt()` is the single place that knows each module's dict shape (defensive `.get()` everywhere), and only serializable scalars cross — the health DataFrame and networkx DiGraph never leak into the Jinja2-consumed payload. Console hardening: stdout/stderr are reconfigured to UTF-8 with errors='replace' so cp1252 CMD consoles never crash on emoji, and legacy loader prints are captured with `redirect_stdout` so model-loading spam never reaches the user.

sections.title: NLP vs fallback, stack, roadmap
sections.explanation: The comparison table summarizes the gate's effect per aspect: sentiment is VADER-only in both modes (the CLI intentionally pins to VADER so a pre-existing transformers install cannot silently change results), emotion exists only when the gate is ON, the narrative is Tier A vs Tier A+Tier B, and health/network are always-on pandas/networkx in both. The tech stack table maps each layer to its tool — hatchling, typer/rich, pandas/numpy, matplotlib/Agg, vendored ECharts, vaderSentiment, networkx, jinja2, requests, and the optional torch/transformers — and notes what was deliberately dropped (plotext, Streamlit, plotly). The closing list is honest about scope: PDF reporting and the Telegram weekly digest ship as modules but are not wired into the CLI, and further export formats are deferred to v2.

pyproject.toml.overview: The packaging file that operationalizes the README's two-tier idea (tour Step 3): a lean core dependency set that every install gets, with the heavy machine-learning stack isolated behind the optional [nlp] extra and dev tooling behind [dev]. It also declares the `chat-analyzer` console script, configures hatchling wheel packaging so the vendored ECharts assets ship, and registers the pytest `slow` marker used by the CI job split.

sections.title: Build system: hatchling
sections.explanation: Declares hatchling >= 1.31.0 as the build backend for PEP 517 builds. Hatchling is chosen for its simple src/-layout support and its `artifacts` glob, which this project needs to force non-code asset files (the vendored ECharts JS bundles) into the wheel — a step you see two sections below.

sections.title: Core metadata and dependencies
sections.explanation: The core contract: name `chat-analyzer-pro`, version 0.1.0, `requires-python = ">=3.11"`, and thirteen always-on dependencies. Read them as layers — pandas/numpy/matplotlib/seaborn for data and static charts, vaderSentiment for the always-on sentiment, networkx for the interaction graph, typer/rich for the CLI, jinja2 for the HTML report, and requests/reportlab/Pillow/wordcloud for the remaining shipped capabilities. What is deliberately absent matters more than what is present: no torch, no transformers — those live in the [nlp] extra, which is why the base install stays small and `--help` stays instant.

sections.title: Optional extras: nlp and dev
sections.explanation: PEP 621 extras in action: `pip install 'chat-analyzer-pro[nlp]'` pulls torch>=2.0, transformers>=4.30,<5.15, and sentencepiece>=0.1.99 only when asked. The comment above the line encodes a real bug fix: transformers does not auto-install sentencepiece, which T5Tokenizer requires, so without it the ANAL-08 summarizer would silently degrade. The `<5.15` upper bound protects against future transformers API breaks. The `dev` extra carries pytest, pytest-cov, and ruff for the CI quality gates from tour Step 13.

sections.title: Console script and wheel assets
sections.explanation: Two wiring points. `[project.scripts]` maps the `chat-analyzer` command straight to the Typer app object at `chat_analyzer.cli:app` — Typer reads the type-annotated `main()` parameters to generate argument parsing and help text automatically. The hatch wheel target packages `src/chat_analyzer` and its `artifacts = ["src/chat_analyzer/assets/*"]` glob is what ships the vendored echarts/echarts-gl bundles inside the wheel, so the HTML report can inline them at render time and stay fully offline.

sections.title: Pytest slow marker
sections.explanation: Registers the custom `slow` marker with a self-describing comment: long wall-clock tests that spawn subprocesses or render the full pipeline. This marker is what lets `pytest -m "not slow"` (documented in the README dev block) run the fast subset locally, while the CI slow job from tour Step 13 runs the full suite in a separate lane.

src/chat_analyzer/__main__.py.overview: The `python -m chat_analyzer` entry point (decision D-02) and the first node of the CLI reading chain in tour Step 4. It does nothing but bind the Typer app from the cli package and, when run as a script, exit with the app's return value — the entire point is to make the package runnable as a module without duplicating any CLI logic.

sections.title: App binding via cli package
sections.explanation: A one-line docstring pins the decision ID (D-02) for traceability with the project's decision log, then imports `app` from `chat_analyzer.cli`. Because `cli/__init__.py` re-exports the same app object that `pyproject.toml`'s `[project.scripts]` entry points at, both invocation styles — the console script and `python -m chat_analyzer` — execute the identical Typer application with zero code duplication.

sections.title: Runnable guard and SystemExit
sections.explanation: The `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard ensures the app runs only when the module is executed directly, not on import. `raise SystemExit(app())` is the idiomatic way to run a Typer app from `python -m`: the app's own return value becomes the process exit status (0 on success, 1 on handled failures), so `python -m chat_analyzer` behaves exactly like the console script in shells and CI. Typer apps are callable objects — that is what makes this pattern work.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/__init__.py.overview: The cli package marker that exposes `app` — the same object that both the `[project.scripts]` console-script target and `__main__.py` bind to (tour Step 4). Its docstring also records the import-cost contract: importing this package pulls only typer and the standard library, which is what keeps `--help`/`--version` instant.

sections.title: Package docstring and contract
sections.explanation: The docstring does real documentation work: it identifies this package as the D-01 console-script target and states the lazy-import guarantee — importing `chat_analyzer.cli` must not pull pandas, matplotlib, or torch. That guarantee is why `--version` and `--help` respond instantly, and it constrains what cli/main.py may import at module level (only typer, stdlib, and the lightweight nlp_gate).

sections.title: App re-export
sections.explanation: Two lines that complete the entry-point wiring: `from .main import app` pulls the Typer instance built in cli/main.py, and `__all__ = ["app"]` makes the re-export explicit for star-imports and tooling. Everything orchestration-related — the tier menu, friendly errors, the re-prompt loop — lives in main.py behind this facade, keeping the package surface minimal.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/main.py.overview: The heart of the CLI (tour Step 4): the Typer app that validates WhatsApp/Telegram/zip export paths, resolves the NLP tier through an interactive 3-option menu or environment overrides, drives `run_pipeline`, writes and auto-opens the HTML report, and converts every failure into a friendly, instructive one-line error — never a traceback. It is also the codebase's natural reading order: a dependency BFS from `__main__.py` reaches exactly these functions first.

sections.title: Docstring, imports, app construction
sections.explanation: The module docstring doubles as a design-contract reference: positional invocation exits 0/1, the no-arg loop re-prompts on ValueError, `--version` needs a custom eager callback because typer 0.27 has no built-in flag, and every interactive run shows the tier menu. The imports prove the laziness claim — only os, sys, pathlib, typer, and the lightweight nlp_gate are loaded at module level. `app = typer.Typer(add_completion=False, ...)` disables the shell-completion option to keep the CLI surface minimal, and the help string is the same one-liner the README uses.

sections.title: Export hints and friendly errors
sections.explanation: Decision D-14 in action: the exact WhatsApp and Telegram export steps are stored as constants and composed into every failure message, so the user learns *how to produce a valid export* at the moment of failure — not a pointer to the README. `_friendly_error()` classifies by exception type and text into four buckets: file-not-found, unsupported file type, empty/unparseable export, and a defensive catch-all. The docstring notes the accompanying invariant: every failure path in main() ends with `typer.Exit(code=1) from None`, so no traceback ever reaches the user.

sections.title: Version callback
sections.explanation: Because typer 0.27 has no built-in `--version`, the D-03 decision implements it as an eager option callback. It reads the version from installed package metadata via `importlib.metadata.version('chat-analyzer-pro')` rather than a hard-coded constant, so the printed version always matches what pip has on disk. The `PackageNotFoundError` branch prints a '(dev)' variant so a source checkout without installation still behaves. Note the lazy import inside the callback — the module keeps its import cost at zero until the flag is actually used.

sections.title: Tier menu and env resolution
sections.explanation: The two halves of tier resolution. `_tier_menu()` is the interactive path (PH2): a 3-option menu with download sizes right in the labels (tier 2 ~0.6 GB, tier 3 ~3 GB), defaulting to 1, with a validation loop that rejects anything but 1/2/3. `_tier_from_env()` is the non-interactive path: `CHAT_ANALYZER_TIER=1|2|3` wins, the legacy `CHAT_ANALYZER_FORCE_NLP` maps 0→1 and 1→3 so existing automation and tests keep working, and the silent default is tier 1. Keeping these as separate pure-ish functions is what makes the non-interactive path testable without a tty.

sections.title: NLP install orchestration
sections.explanation: The pre-analysis readiness step for tiers 2/3. `_announce_install()` implements the D-05 announce-then-construct rule — names and sizes (torch flavor plus both model IDs with MB sizes from nlp_gate) are printed before any pip run, so a multi-GB download never looks like a frozen terminal. `_ensure_nlp_for_tier()` maps `nlp_gate.nlp_status()` onto actions: READY proceeds silently, MISSING installs the tier's flavor then downloads both models, OUTDATED asks the user whether to update (and on a non-tty just continues with what is installed). Every `RuntimeError` from the gate is caught and converted into a warning plus 'Continuing with basic analysis' and a False return — a failed install degrades the run instead of killing it.

sections.title: Per-path analysis and report
sections.explanation: The single body shared by both invocation styles. All heavy imports happen here — rich Console, run_pipeline, stage_status, render, and the report writer — which is exactly the lazy-import boundary the docstring promised. After the pipeline returns, the function prints the `Messages: N` count line: the D-05 smoke-contract token printed exactly once, here, so pipeline.py and render.py must never print a second one (a Phase-1 smoke test pins this). Then the report is written inside a `stage_status` spinner, `report_path` is stored back into the results dict, the rich summary panel renders, and the browser auto-open is attempted.

sections.title: Command signature and console bootstrap
sections.explanation: The `@app.command()` decorated `main()` is the app root: `chat_file` is an optional positional argument (the `# noqa: B008` acknowledges the Typer idiom that argument defaults must be `typer.Argument()` calls), and `--version` is an eager option wired to the callback. The first thing the command body does is the Windows console bootstrap: both stdout and stderr are reconfigured to UTF-8 with errors='replace' so a default cp1252 CMD console cannot crash on emoji in chat text — the guard catches AttributeError/ValueError from non-standard stream objects. A rich Console is then constructed for all subsequent output.

sections.title: NLP resolution per run
sections.explanation: The nested `_resolve_nlp()` closure returns `(nlp_enabled, menu_shown)` for the current run. On a tty it first runs the Windows long-path guard — warning *before* the menu offers a multi-GB download that could die with WinError 206 — then always shows the menu regardless of install state. On a non-tty it uses `_tier_from_env()` and never prompts. Tiers 2/3 in both paths delegate to `_ensure_nlp_for_tier()`, so the readiness logic lives in exactly one place. The `menu_shown` flag matters later: it gates the post-run NLP hint so users who already saw the menu are not nagged again.

sections.title: Positional path branch
sections.explanation: The direct-invocation path. Two cheap pre-checks happen before anything heavy: existence (with a friendly FileNotFoundError message) and extension membership in {.txt, .json, .zip} — anything else gets the 'Unsupported file type' line, both exiting 1. The pipeline runs inside a try that catches ValueError (the parsers' contract for a malformed/empty export) and converts it to a friendly line with `raise ... from None`, suppressing the traceback chain. After success, the D-06 hint — a single soft-wrapped ASCII line pointing at `pip install chat-analyzer-pro\[nlp]` — prints only when the user never saw the menu, then the command exits 0 explicitly.

sections.title: Interactive re-prompt loop
sections.explanation: The no-argument path is a loop that re-prompts until it gets a usable path: quotes are stripped from pasted paths, existence and extension are validated with the same friendly errors, and a ValueError from analysis loops back for another try (decision D-15 — a bad file never exits the interactive session). Success follows the identical sequence as the positional branch — resolve NLP, analyze, hint, exit 0. The `if __name__ == "__main__": app()` tail makes the module itself runnable, though the supported paths are the console script and `python -m`. Note the symmetry: both branches share `_resolve_nlp`, `_analyze_path`, and the hint logic, which is why they stay behaviorally identical.

src/chat_analyzer/ingest/ingestion.py.overview: The input dispatcher (tour Step 5): it recognizes every supported input — WhatsApp .txt, Telegram-style JSON, ZIP archives, screenshots via OCR, and PDFs with an OCR fallback — normalizes raw messages into the canonical message schema, and builds the canonical analysis DataFrame with honest skip counting. It carries both the modern pipeline API (`messages_to_dataframe`, `normalize_message`) and the legacy `process_uploaded_file()` library API with its dependency-gated OCR/PDF helpers.

sections.title: Docstring, imports, logger
sections.explanation: The module docstring declares the public API and the feature list — all file formats, OCR extraction, PDF with OCR fallback, and graceful dependency fallbacks. Imports are stdlib plus pandas only, which keeps the module importable even in the lean base install. The logger is created with a `NullHandler` so library-style logging never spams the console — a convention the whole package follows (it is why `logger.exception` noise stays silent during pipeline runs).

sections.title: Optional dependency flags
sections.explanation: Four guarded imports (PIL, pytesseract, pdfplumber, pdf2image) each set a flag in the DEPENDENCIES dict instead of failing the import. This is the graceful-degradation pattern for optional features: OCR and PDF support simply turn off when the libraries are missing, logging an info line rather than raising. Note the `ImageFile.LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES = True` tweak — real-world screenshot uploads are often truncated, and PIL would otherwise refuse to open them. Consumers check `get_dependency_status()` or the flags before using these paths.

sections.title: Date patterns, regex, extensions
sections.explanation: The module's format knowledge in constants. `WHATSAPP_DATE_PATTERNS` enumerates eight strptime layouts (DD/MM vs MM/DD, 2/4-digit years, 12h vs 24h). `WAP_MESSAGE_RE` is the verbose regex that matches a WhatsApp line into date, time, author, and text groups, tolerating an optional comma and optional AM/PM. The three extension sets classify images, audio, video, and the union MEDIA_EXTENSIONS, which the ZIP and dispatch logic use for routing. These constants serve the legacy `parse_whatsapp_text` path; the strict parser in parser/whatsapp_parser.py has its own faster machinery.

sections.title: Dependency status and datetime parse
sections.explanation: `get_dependency_status()` is a tiny introspection helper returning a copy of the flags dict (safe against callers mutating it). `try_parse_datetime()` is the best-effort date parser for WhatsApp-ish strings: it tries three candidate normalizations of the raw string against all eight patterns, then falls back to a regex that rebuilds a canonical `date, time` string and retries — on total failure it returns the original string and an empty time, never raising. The `# noqa: DTZ007` comments document a deliberate choice: WhatsApp exports carry no timezone, so naive datetimes are accepted here and normalized to naive UTC downstream.

sections.title: WhatsApp text parser
sections.explanation: A classic streaming state machine for multiline messages: when a line matches `WAP_MESSAGE_RE` the current message is flushed and a new one starts; non-matching lines are appended as continuations of the current message (with a newline join) or, if no message is open yet, become 'orphan' records with an unknown author so the text is never silently lost. Empty lines append a bare newline to preserve message-internal blank lines. The trailing flush after the loop handles the final message. Each record keeps `date_raw`/`time_raw` rather than a parsed datetime — parsing is deferred to `normalize_message`, which keeps this parser tolerant of partially unparseable lines.

sections.title: JSON parsing and OCR/PDF helpers
sections.explanation: `parse_json_chat()` accepts bytes, str, or a file-like object, decodes defensively (errors='ignore'), and walks three shapes: a dict with a `messages` list (Telegram bare export), a dict with `chats` whose messages are flattened (full export), or a bare top-level list — returning None (never raising) for anything else. The OCR helpers follow the same degrade-never-crash discipline: `ocr_image_bytes` returns '' when PIL/pytesseract are missing or extraction fails; `extract_text_from_pdf` walks pages with pdfplumber, falls back to `_ocr_pdf_page` (rasterize via pdf2image, then tesseract) for image-only pages or failures, and tags each page's provenance with `[page:N]`/`[ocr]` markers. Every failure path logs and degrades rather than aborting the whole ingestion.

sections.title: Media metadata and UTC normalizer
sections.explanation: `extract_media_metadata()` classifies a file by extension into audio/video/unknown and computes size fields including a human-readable string via `_format_file_size` (a simple B→KB→MB→GB→TB ladder). `_to_naive_utc()` is the single datetime normalization contract shared with the parser boundary: strings go through `datetime.fromisoformat` (Python 3.11 accepts a trailing 'Z' natively, so no string surgery is needed), tz-aware values are shifted to UTC and stripped of tzinfo, naive values pass through unchanged. Unparseable input raises — nothing is silently fabricated — leaving the decision to the caller.

sections.title: Canonical DataFrame and message schema
sections.explanation: The two functions that define the canonical schema. `messages_to_dataframe()` is THE dict→df builder for the whole pipeline: it resolves a datetime from `datetime`/`timestamp`/ISO `date`/`date + time` fields, drops rows that fail (counted when `return_counts=True` so drops are visible to parse statistics — the COR-02 fix for previously-silent losses), and emits the full column set: datetime, timestamp (an alias the chart visualizer requires), date, hour, sender (author/sender/from with an 'unknown' fallback), message, message_length, source, and a uid (existing id or a fresh uuid4). `normalize_message()` maps any raw dict into the standard normalized schema {uid, date, time, author, text, source, media, meta}, trying `try_parse_datetime` for raw date strings and `_to_naive_utc` for datetime objects, and stashing a `_raw_preview` in meta for debugging. Together they make 'one row per message' true regardless of which parser produced the dicts.

sections.title: process_uploaded_file dispatcher
sections.explanation: The legacy main entry (the library API predating the CLI). `_read_file_content()` handles three upload shapes — a Streamlit-style object with .name/.read(), a (name, bytes) tuple, or a filesystem path. `process_uploaded_file()` then routes by extension to per-type processors, and this is where the honest-counting style shows: any read or processing failure returns a note record instead of raising. After dispatch, every raw message goes through `normalize_message()` with a per-message try/except that substitutes a fallback record (flagged `_normalization_error: True`) rather than losing the whole batch to one malformed message. The return value pairs normalized messages with media analysis results (OCR text, PDF text, media metadata).

sections.title: Type processors and demo block
sections.explanation: The per-type internals behind the dispatcher. `_process_zip_file()` iterates archive members and re-dispatches each to the right processor — text and JSON members become messages, images/PDFs go through OCR, media files yield metadata, and unknown members get a note; a failing member degrades to a logged warning and a corrupt archive is reported via the media list. The remaining helpers tag `source_hint` values (whatsapp_txt, json, ocr_image, pdf, generic_text) which later surface as the DataFrame's `source` column. `get_supported_formats()` is an introspection endpoint, and the `__main__` block is a manual demo that prints dependency status, supported formats, and the first few parsed messages — the quickest way to smoke-test this module by hand.

src/chat_analyzer/parser/whatsapp_parser.overview: The WhatsApp specialist (tour Step 5): a regex-based line parser that classifies each export line as a message, a system line, or a skip — with honest counters and never a fabricated timestamp. Its headline trick is the strict datetime fast path that eliminated 3.8 million `strptime()` calls on the 424k-message benchmark chat; a legacy DataFrame path with media/emoji/time features is kept for backward compatibility.

sections.title: Date formats and fast-path regex
sections.explanation: The constants encode a subtle correctness decision (C-17): `DATE_FORMATS` tries day-first (%d/%m) before month-first, because the dominant DD/MM/YYYY export format parses correctly there, while a US-first order would silently misread dates like 02/11/25 as Feb 11 whenever the day ≤ 12. The 16 variants cover 2/4-digit years, seconds, 12h AM/PM, and 24h clocks. `_FIXED_SHAPE` is the fast-path regex for canonical 'DD/MM/YY HH:MM[AM/PM]' strings, and `_NOT_HANDLED` is a sentinel object — distinct from None — so the caller can distinguish 'shape not recognized, run strptime fallback' from 'recognized but invalid'.

sections.title: Parser init: patterns and counters
sections.explanation: The constructor assembles five regexes. `message_pattern` matches the plain 'date time - sender: text' layout with an optional-seconds group and optional AM/PM; the `:\s?(.*)` tail makes the whitespace after the colon optional so empty-body messages (deleted or media-removed lines ending in just the sender) still count as real messages instead of falling through to system lines. `alt_pattern` handles the iOS bracketed '[dd/mm/yy, hh:mm] sender: text' style. Three system-line patterns follow (D-18): any header without a sender, bare system phrases like 'X added Y', and the end-to-end encryption notice. The three counters (skipped/system/total) are initialized here and reset per parse — they are instance state so the report can read them after parsing.

sections.title: Strict datetime fast path
sections.explanation: The performance centerpiece. `_parse_datetime_strict()` first tries `_parse_fast` — a hand-rolled conversion for canonical shapes that mirrors the strptime loop exactly (2-digit years map POSIX-style, 12h requires hour 1–12 and uppercase AM/PM, minute/second ranges are validated, ambiguous day/month is tried day-first first) — and only falls back to the 16-format strptime loop for strings outside the fast shape. This is what took per-parse `strptime()` calls from 3.8M to zero on the benchmark chat. The 'strict' in the name matters too: total failure returns None, never a fabricated current timestamp — corrupt dates must be counted as skipped (D-15). The `# noqa` comments document that naive datetimes are deliberate and normalized downstream.

sections.title: Line classification
sections.explanation: `parse_line_strict()` is the single-line classifier the report path uses: try the plain pattern, then the bracketed iOS one; on a header match, build the timestamp string (defaulting '00:00' when seconds-only forms lack a time), parse strictly, and on failure count a skip and return None. A successful match returns the full row shape — datetime, sender, message, message_length, type, date, time, hour, day_of_week, word_count — which is the dict the architecture doc documents as the parser-level row. Unmatched lines are then checked against the encryption notice, the system-header pattern, and the system-phrase pattern (only for lines ≤ 120 chars, a cheap guard against false positives) — each increments `system_messages` and returns None. `parse_line()` is the legacy shim that renames 'datetime' to 'timestamp' for old callers.

sections.title: File parse with honest counters
sections.explanation: The file-level engine the pipeline actually calls. It opens with `encoding='utf-8-sig'` (strips the BOM WhatsApp exports start with) and errors='replace' (a stray byte never kills the run), resets the counters, and streams line by line. The control flow is a small state machine: a parsed line flushes the previous message and starts a new one; a line that merely incremented `system_messages` or `skipped_lines` is detected by comparing the counters before/after the call and skipped as a continuation; any other non-empty line becomes a continuation of the current multiline message (updating message_length and word_count), or, if no message is open, an honest orphan skip (D-16). The return value is the parser-boundary contract: `(rows, counts)` with total_lines, parsed_messages, skipped_lines, system_messages.

sections.title: Legacy parse_file wrapper
sections.explanation: The QUAL-01 compatibility entry point: it delegates to `parse_file_with_report()`, builds a DataFrame, and renames 'datetime' to 'timestamp' so the existing `_add_features` pipeline keeps working. Note the empty-frame guard — `pd.DataFrame([])` has no columns to rename, so the rename and feature pass are skipped. This method exists for notebook/scripts-style usage; the CLI pipeline goes through rows + counts and the ingest builder instead, keeping the DataFrame construction in exactly one place.

sections.title: Feature enrichment and time buckets
sections.explanation: `_add_features()` is the legacy enrichment pass that `example_parsed.csv`'s richer cousins come from: rows are sorted by timestamp and given a sequence number, `is_media` is a case-insensitive contains over the seven WhatsApp media placeholders ('<Media omitted>', 'image omitted', ...), and `emoji_count` counts matches of a hand-built emoji-range regex (with `has_emoji` as its boolean shadow). Time features follow: `is_weekend` from pandas' dayofweek and `time_period` bucketed Morning/Afternoon/Evening/Night by `_categorize_time_period` (5–12, 12–17, 17–21, else Night). These derived columns exist so EDA and charts can group without recomputing.

sections.title: CSV save and basic stats
sections.explanation: Two legacy conveniences. `save_processed_data()` creates the output directory if needed and writes the DataFrame to CSV — this is literally the code that produced `data/processed/example_parsed.csv` from the bundled sample, and it prints the destination path. `get_basic_stats()` returns the summary dict (total messages, date range, participants, per-participant counts, media count, total words, average length, total emojis) or an error dict for an empty frame; the free-function demo at the bottom prints it as the 'WhatsApp Chat Analysis Summary' block.

sections.title: Utility function and demo
sections.explanation: `parse_whatsapp_chat()` bundles the whole legacy flow: parse, optionally save to CSV, print the stats summary, and return the DataFrame — the one-liner a notebook user reaches for. The `__main__` block hard-codes the project's demo paths (the bundled sample in, `data/processed/example_parsed.csv` out), which is exactly how the committed example CSV was generated; run this file directly and you reproduce it. The missing-file branch prints a helpful message pointing at the sample directory rather than raising.

src/chat_analyzer/parser/telegram_parser.overview: The Telegram specialist (tour Step 5): parses both JSON export shapes (bare chat and full export), recursively joins entity-array message texts, filters service messages, normalizes tz-aware dates to naive UTC, and counts every dropped message honestly. Its public contract mirrors the WhatsApp parser exactly — `(rows, counts)` from the report function, a DataFrame from the legacy wrapper.

sections.title: Docstring and imports
sections.explanation: The module docstring states the four responsibilities and two policy decisions by ID: D-19 (honest counting, no bare `except: continue`) and D-20 (naive UTC normalization). Imports are minimal — json, datetime (with the 3.11 UTC alias), pandas, and requests for the URL-loading variant. Notably there is no regex state machine here: Telegram exports are structured JSON, so the parser walks dicts rather than lines.

sections.title: Message extraction from both shapes
sections.explanation: `_load_messages()` handles both export shapes Telegram Desktop produces: a bare chat export (top-level `"messages": [...]`) and a full export (`"chats": [{"messages": [...]}]`), flattening every chat's messages into one list. The ValueError raising is deliberate (MEDIUM #3): an empty or non-Telegram JSON must fail loudly with a data-shape error so the CLI can show its 'No messages could be parsed' friendly message — the comment records that ValueError (not TypeError) is the contract because this is a data-shape failure. Two raise sites cover 'neither key present' and 'present but empty'.

sections.title: Entity-array text joining
sections.explanation: Telegram represents message text either as a plain string or as an array of parts, where formatting entities (bold, links, mentions) appear as dicts carrying their own `text`. `_join_text()` accepts both: strings pass through, list parts are appended in order, and dict parts contribute their `text` value while parts without one are skipped. Anything else yields an empty string. This recursion is what keeps styled messages readable instead of dropping their text entirely.

sections.title: Naive UTC normalization
sections.explanation: The D-20 contract, identical to the helper of the same name in ingest/ingestion.py: parse an ISO string with `datetime.fromisoformat` (Python 3.11 handles the trailing 'Z' natively, noted via the ruff FURB162 reference), shift tz-aware values to UTC and strip tzinfo, and let naive values through. Telegram dates are tz-aware ISO strings, so in practice this converts export-local timestamps to UTC — the single convention the entire analysis stack assumes.

sections.title: Report-based parse loop
sections.explanation: The main function. Loading supports both a file path and an http(s) URL (requests + response.json()). The loop classifies every message: `type == 'service'` (joins, pins, invites) increments system_messages and is excluded from rows; any other non-'message' type is an honest skip; a missing or unparseable date is a caught skip rather than a crash (each except branch increments skipped_lines — no bare except: continue, per D-19). Messages with media but no text get the '<Media omitted>' placeholder so they still count as content rows, matching what WhatsApp exports show naturally. The sender falls back from `from` to `actor` (service-adjacent sends) to 'Unknown', an optional `message_id` rides along when present, and the returned counts dict mirrors the WhatsApp parser's four keys exactly — which is what lets ingestion treat both formats identically.

sections.title: DataFrame wrapper
sections.explanation: The legacy entry point: call the report function, discard the counts, and wrap the rows in a DataFrame. Its docstring records the hardening history — service rows excluded, malformed messages counted and dropped, empty exports now raising ValueError from `_load_messages` where they previously returned an empty DataFrame that downstream code would choke on. The CLI pipeline uses the report variant; this wrapper serves scripts and tests that just want a frame.

data/sample_chats/whatsapp_sample.txt.overview: The bundled WhatsApp demo export (tour Step 5): a 28-message, two-participant conversation between Alice and Bob over three days (Dec 25–27, 2023). It is the exact input the README quickstart replays, the fixture behind the golden-parity tests (27 parsed messages in Step 12's expectations), and a deliberately crafted exercise for the parser: a multiline message, two `<Media omitted>` placeholders, emoji, and an AM/PM 12-hour clock in the US-style month-first date layout.

sections.title: Day 1: greeting exchange
sections.explanation: The opening exchange establishes the format the parser must handle: '12/25/23, 9:30 AM - Alice: ...' — month-first MM/DD/YY with a comma, 12-hour clock with AM, then the ' - ' separator. Line 1 carries emoji (🎄🎅) that the emoji-count regex and top-emoji stats pick up. Lines 3–4 demonstrate the multiline case: 'Family time is the best ❤️' has no timestamp header, so `parse_file_with_report()` treats it as a continuation of Alice's 9:35 message — which is why the parsed CSV shows one 73-character message instead of two rows. Note the header line is a message header, not a system line: it has a sender after the dash.

sections.title: Media placeholders and photos
sections.explanation: This stretch exercises the media story: lines 6 and 10 are literal '<Media omitted>' placeholders — the string WhatsApp writes when a chat is exported without media — and the parser's `is_media` pattern list matches them exactly, so they count as messages while the analysis marks them as media. Lines 7–9 and 11–13 form the conversational pattern around the placeholders (offering a photo, reacting to it), which gives the sample a natural reply rhythm for the relationship-health and network analyses. The afternoon timestamps (2:30 PM → 14:30 in the parsed CSV) show the 12h→24h conversion the strict parser performs.

sections.title: Day 2: morning catch-up
sections.explanation: The second day provides the multi-day span that date-range and daily-timeline statistics need. The quick back-and-forth (8:30/8:31, 9:00/9:01, 10:00/10:15) produces the short response lags the relationship-health module's response-pattern analysis feeds on. Emoji appear again (🍿, 😄) and the message lengths vary from 14 to 56 characters, giving the length-averaging stats something to bite on. This is also the block where both participants alternate strictly, useful for the initiator-balance metrics.

sections.title: Day 3: wind-down and newline
sections.explanation: The final day closes the conversation with the 7:00–8:15 morning sequence and a 👋 sign-off, completing the three-day span (Dec 25–27) the date-range stats report. The trailing blank line (line 29) is harmless — the parser skips empty lines before counting `total_lines`, which is why the golden fixtures record 27 parsed messages from 28 content lines: no header/encryption/system lines exist in this sample, so every counted line parses. As a fixture it is stable and tiny, which is exactly what the golden-parity test wants.

data/sample_chats/telegram_sample.json.overview: The bundled Telegram demo export (tour Step 5): a bare-chat-shape JSON (top-level "messages" array) with five messages from a three-person project-team chat. It is the input the README quickstart suggests for the Telegram path and the fixture that exercises `_load_messages` (bare shape), `_join_text` (plain-string texts), the naive-UTC date normalization, and the honest type filtering in telegram_parser.py.

sections.title: Chat metadata header
sections.explanation: The top-level keys are what make this a Telegram Desktop export: `name` ('Telegram Chat with Project Team'), `type: "personal_chat"`, and a numeric chat `id`. None of these are consumed by the parser — `_load_messages()` looks only for `messages` (or `chats`) and deliberately raises ValueError when neither exists, so a JSON file without this structure gets the CLI's friendly 'No messages could be parsed' error rather than silently parsing to zero messages. The `messages` array opening at line 5 is where the bare-chat shape is confirmed.

sections.title: First messages: repo thread
sections.explanation: Messages 1–3 show the per-message schema the parser walks: numeric `id`, `type: "message"` (the value the service-message filter compares against), a naive ISO `date` ('2025-09-15T09:45:00', no timezone offset — so `_to_naive_utc` passes it through unchanged), `from` as the sender (with `actor` as the parser's fallback), and `text` as a plain string, which `_join_text()` returns as-is. The three participants — Sujoy, Ravi, Ananya — turn this into the group-chat case, so participant breakdowns and per-sender stats have more than two buckets to work with.

sections.title: Closing messages and closure
sections.explanation: Messages 4–5 complete the thread (a plan to push test cases and finalize) and demonstrate one real-world wrinkle: message 5's text contains the escaped Unicode `\u2019` right single quote in 'Let\u2019s' — standard JSON escaping that `json.load` decodes transparently. The array and object close cleanly at lines 41–42. Note what is absent by design: no `type: "service"` entries, no entity-array texts, no photo/video keys in this fixture — those richer paths (service filtering, '<Media omitted>' synthesis, entity joining) are exercised by the parser's own unit tests rather than this minimal sample.

data/processed/example_parsed.csv.overview: The worked example of the canonical data contract (tour Step 6): the WhatsApp sample after parsing, one row per message with the canonical columns datetime, sender, message, date, time, hour, and message_length. It was produced by running `whatsapp_parser.py`'s demo block against `data/sample_chats/whatsapp_sample.txt`, and it is the shape every analysis module in the tour's Step 8 expects as input — follow one message from the sample .txt and this is where it lands.

sections.title: Header: canonical columns
sections.explanation: The single header row names the canonical schema the tour's Step 6 calls out: `datetime` (tz-naive combined timestamp), `sender`, `message`, `date`, `time`, `hour`, and `message_length`. Every downstream module — ChatEDA, sentiment, relationship health, network — keys off exactly these names, which is why the ingest builder and both parsers agree on them. The CLI pipeline's richer frame adds columns (source, uid, timestamp alias) on top of this base set, so this file is the minimal common denominator.

sections.title: Day 1 rows: parsing effects
sections.explanation: The Dec 25 rows show every transformation the parser applies. The 9:35 row is the multiline case: the continuation line was joined with a space and folded into one 73-character message. The '<Media omitted>' rows (10:16, 14:30) are preserved verbatim as message text — they count as messages but carry the media marker the analysis layer detects. Timestamps are converted from the export's 12-hour clock to 24-hour datetimes (2:30 PM → 14:30), and `hour` is extracted as its own integer column for peak-hour stats, while `time` keeps the HH:MM:SS string form. `message_length` counts characters of the final message text, matching the 19-char 'Merry Christmas! 🎄🎅' row.

sections.title: Day 2-3 rows and CSV quoting
sections.explanation: The Dec 26–27 rows complete the 27-message span and demonstrate RFC-4180 quoting: row 16 ("Morning! It was great, played some games with the family") is double-quoted because its text contains a comma, which pandas' `to_csv` emits automatically. Compare this file with the sample .txt row-for-row and the parser's guarantees become checkable by eye: 28 header-less content lines become 27 messages (the multiline join), no rows are dropped, and timestamps stay chronological across all three days. This predictability is what makes the golden-parity test suite able to pin exact expected aggregates from a fixture like this.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/contracts.py.overview: The interface-contract module of the CLI layer: one small file where both the ParseReport counters and the full AnalysisResults payload are defined. Its docstring stakes out the single-source-of-truth role — pipeline.py, adapters.py, render.py and report_html.py all consume these types, while the analysis core (parser/ingest/analysis) never imports this module. That split keeps the analysis engine CLI-agnostic: parsers return plain counts dicts, and only pipeline.py wraps them into a ParseReport. Tour Step 6 introduces this file as the shared vocabulary the pipeline (Step 7) and the HTML report (Step 11) both speak.

sections.title: Contract role and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring sets the architectural rule before any code: this module is the single source of truth for the CLI's data shapes, and the analysis core must never import it. Parsers hand back plain dicts of counters, and pipeline.py is the one that constructs a ParseReport from them. The imports are deliberately tiny — only dataclass and typing helpers — because a contract module must not drag heavy dependencies into whoever imports it.

sections.title: ParseReport dataclass
sections.explanation: ParseReport aggregates the parse counters for one export file: total lines, parsed messages, skipped lines, system messages and media messages. Every counter defaults to 0 so partially-filled reports stay valid, and source records which parser produced the row set. This is the typed shape the pipeline prints its parsed-count narration from and that adapters.py later flattens into the parse block of AnalysisResults.

sections.title: AnalysisResults TypedDict
sections.explanation: AnalysisResults is a TypedDict — a plain dict whose keys are statically checkable — describing the complete payload run_pipeline produces: stats, participants, content, sentiment, health, network, narrative, gated emotion, charts (base64 PNG data URIs), charts_json (ECharts option dicts), insights and report_path. The docstring records the non-obvious rules: charts_json falls back to the PNG charts when a JSON spec build fails, narrative is ALWAYS present because Tier A is always-on, and emotion is None when the silent availability probe says the NLP models are unusable. Health and network deliberately hold only serializable scalars — never the raw prepared_data DataFrame or the networkx DiGraph (Pattern 3). report_path stays empty until main.py fills it after the report is written.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/adapters.py.overview: The anti-corruption layer between the analysis engine and the CLI contract (Research Pattern 2): this file is the ONLY place that knows each analysis module's internal dict shape. adapt() assembles the full AnalysisResults contract from those raw dicts, and every access is a defensive .get() so an empty edge-case dict never raises KeyError here. The _build_* helpers extract only JSON-serializable scalars — never the prepared_data DataFrame or the networkx DiGraph — and build_insights formats the per-tab narrative lead-ins from the stats alone. Tour Step 6 positions this file as the single place raw analysis results get translated into the typed contract.

sections.title: Anti-corruption layer header
sections.explanation: The module docstring names its pattern explicitly: this file alone knows the internal shapes of ChatEDA summaries, sentiment summaries and visualizer charts, and every access must be a defensive .get(). It imports the two contract types plus non_latin_message_share, which later annotates insights for substantially non-English chats. Keeping all shape knowledge here means the analysis modules can evolve their dict keys without touching the report renderer.

sections.title: adapt signature and guarantees
sections.explanation: adapt() takes the source label, ParseReport, canonical DataFrame and the three always-on analysis dicts positionally; health, network, emotion, narrative and charts_json are keyword-only with None defaults. That keyword-only shape was a reconciliation decision: direct-call tests from Phase 2 stay green while the pipeline passes richer data. The narrative block is always present — a default empty Tier-A-shaped dict is used when the caller passes nothing, so the report can always read the tab.

sections.title: Building the stats block
sections.explanation: This block derives report-facing top-level stats from the canonical DataFrame: participant list, date range, duration days, busiest day (the column-sum max of the hourly activity matrix), peak hour and average response time — with a single-message chat's NaT response time normalized to None (LOW #9). The media_messages computation is the subtle part (D3/P17): zip exports carry real media FILES while plain exports carry '<Media omitted>' marker rows, and in a real WhatsApp export the two are the same messages, so summing would double-count. max() of the two counts is therefore the honest total, and it gracefully covers Telegram zips (files, no markers) and plain .txt exports (markers, no files).

sections.title: Participants and content blocks
sections.explanation: Participants are sorted descending by message count, each carrying messages, average message length and a percentage share rounded to one decimal — the exact shape the report's participant table renders. The content block converts the module's Counter objects into plain lists via most_common(15): top words, top emojis, total and unique word counts. The `or Counter()` fallbacks are the defensive pattern in action: a content module returning an empty dict still yields a valid empty block.

sections.title: Sentiment block extraction
sections.explanation: The sentiment block pulls four fields from the sentiment summary: the distribution (counts per Positive/Neutral/Negative), the mean VADER compound, per-sender sentiment and daily average sentiment from the temporal analysis. Keys are coerced to str and counts to int so the dict is JSON-serializable for the report. Every lookup is chained through `or {}` so a missing temporal_analysis key degrades to an empty daily series instead of a crash.

sections.title: Assembling the contract
sections.explanation: This is where the always-on vs gated blocks are wired: health and network blocks are built only when the caller passed data, the emotion block only when the NLP stage produced a summary, and the narrative block is normalized unconditionally. The comment re-states Pattern 3: the health module returns a prepared_data DataFrame and the network module a DiGraph plus interaction matrix — neither may leak into AnalysisResults, so only serializable scalars are extracted. The final AnalysisResults(...) call assembles everything, delegating insights to build_insights and leaving report_path empty for main.py to fill after the report is written.

sections.title: Health block extractor
sections.explanation: _build_health_block maps the health module's nested dicts onto nine flat serializable fields: overall score, grade, component scores (accepting either key spelling), initiator balance, conversation count, average response minutes, response balance and composite dominance. The docstring stresses the DataFrame never crosses this boundary because the block is consumed directly by Jinja templates. This flat mapping is what the report's health tab reads without knowing the module's internals.

sections.title: Network block and tie-aware summary
sections.explanation: _build_network_block extracts node/edge counts, density, reciprocity (trying two possible key locations), strongest connections, key participants and the subgroup count. The helper _strongest_connection_summary solves a two-person-chat honesty problem (WS-3): in a pair chat both directions of a sender switch tie at the same count, so naming 'A to B' as strongest would be arbitrary — when the top two edges are mirror images with equal weight it returns 'Evenly matched: N turn-exchanges in each direction' instead. This wording is what build_insights and the report both reuse.

sections.title: Emotion and narrative normalizers
sections.explanation: _build_emotion_block derives the dominant emotion itself from the distribution when the module's summary lacks a dominant key, and passes through the Option C sampling metadata (scored/total/cap) so the report can label results as based on a sample of N of M messages, plus per-quarter emotion rows for the quarterly timeline chart. _build_narrative_block accepts three caller shapes — a Tier A result, a pipeline block with Tier B filled in, or nothing — and coerces every observation into {text, confidence, kind}, stringifying plain-text observations. The no-narrative default is a fully-formed empty Tier A dict so older result files without the key never KeyError in the renderer.

sections.title: build_insights lead-ins
sections.explanation: build_insights formats one natural-language lead-in per report tab (D-11), driven entirely by the stats values — no hardcoded numbers and never the string 'None'. The sentences follow fixed tab order: busiest day, top participant, response time, top word, tone, then health and network (with the health estimate explicitly qualified as speculative, B4), then emotion, duration and peak hour. When the chat is 30% or more non-Latin (WS-4) the sentiment and emotion sentences get an appended honesty disclaimer noting the models are English-only, and the final return truncates to at most 11 insights so tab indices never shift.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/pipeline.py.overview: The busiest node in the project graph: run_pipeline is the ONLY orchestration path, taking one export file from parse to the full AnalysisResults contract. It detects the input type (.txt WhatsApp, .json Telegram, .zip archive), parses into the canonical DataFrame, then drives every analysis stage in order — EDA, sentiment, relationship health, network, charts, narrative and the gated NLP emotion/narrative stages — before adapters.adapt() maps everything into the contract. The file encodes standing rules: matplotlib is pinned to the Agg backend lazily before any pyplot import, analysis-module stdout is captured so prints never reach the user, chart failures degrade to empty strings, and narration degrades from a live rich progress bar on a TTY to plain '[OK]' lines when piped. Tour Step 7 walks this file as the place where a run comes together.

sections.title: Orchestration rules and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring enumerates the design rules the file honors: lazy matplotlib with Agg pinned first (Pitfall 7), lazy analysis-module imports inside a stdout-capturing stage (Pitfall 5), chart crashes degrading instead of killing the report, and tty/off-tty narration (D-12/Pitfall 8). Imports stay deliberately light — chart_json, contracts and the DataFrame builder — because everything heavier is imported inside run_pipeline. This keeps `import pipeline` cheap even on a lean base install.

sections.title: Chart encoding helpers
sections.explanation: fig_to_data_uri renders a matplotlib figure into a base64 PNG data URI at 120 dpi and closes the figure so figures never leak between runs. _safe_chart wraps it in a try/except that logs the traceback and substitutes an empty string — a chart crash must never kill the report (Pitfall 6). The report template then simply skips empty chart slots.

sections.title: Stage narration helpers
sections.explanation: stage_status shows a rich Status spinner on a real terminal but degrades to a plain '[OK] <label>' line when stdout is piped, because rich renders nothing off-tty. stage() is the progress-bar-aware variant: when a rich Progress exists it advances the task's description by one step, otherwise it falls back to stage_status. The labels are pinned strings ('Parsing chat', 'Computing insights', ...) that a test asserts verbatim, so narration text is part of the contract.

sections.title: Tier B digest and sanity gate
sections.explanation: _tier_b_digest composes the compact ASCII digest the generative narrative summarizes: the Tier A observation texts plus one factual fallback line — never raw chat messages, keeping the model's input tiny and private (B5). _acceptable_narrative_text is the WS-6 sanity gate for Tier B output: sane length (5-250 chars), no code-like tokens (brackets, def, import, =>) and must end like a sentence. Garbage model output is therefore never surfaced.

sections.title: run_pipeline setup and NLP probe
sections.explanation: run_pipeline pins matplotlib to Agg immediately — before anything imports pyplot — then runs the silent NLP availability probe once up front (D-02/D-05) so the progress task total matches the stages actually run. The CLI's tier menu forces nlp_enabled True/False from main.py, while None keeps the old auto-detect probe for direct and test callers. On a terminal a determinate rich Progress bar starts with total 4 (NLP on) or 3; off-tty the helper degrades to plain lines.

sections.title: Parsing stage and canonical DataFrame
sections.explanation: Inside the 'Parsing chat' stage the file suffix picks the parser: WhatsAppParser for .txt, the Telegram parser for .json, and zip_input for .zip (which returns rows/counts in the same contract shape plus the chosen transcript names). The parsed count and participant count print immediately, followed by an honest skipped-lines warning. messages_to_dataframe then builds the canonical DataFrame, surfacing COR-02's dropped rows (missing datetime) separately from the parsers' own skip tally, and an empty frame raises a clean ValueError.

sections.title: Sample cap prompt and cache lookup
sections.explanation: When NLP is on and the scorable message count exceeds the emotion sample cap (Option C), the pipeline prompts on an interactive terminal with default NO (exact scoring) and auto-samples on piped/CI runs; the effective cap rides in the cache key so answering y and N on the same file produce distinct entries. The result cache (04-08) is then consulted: cache_key mixes the file hash with nlp_on, sample cap, worker count and chosen zip transcripts; on a hit the whole compute is skipped and the cached payload returned. Both knobs resolve through nlp_gate, keeping the environment story in one module.

sections.title: Computing insights stage
sections.explanation: The 'Computing insights' stage runs inside a redirect_stdout capture so analysis-module prints never reach the user. The CLI pins TRANSFORMERS_AVAILABLE=False before importing sentiment (plan contract A6): a stray transformers install in the environment must not load an HF model on every run. ChatEDA's three analyzers plus summary run, VADER sentiment is added, and the always-on relationship-health and network modules (pandas/numpy/networkx only) compute inside the same capture. Six PNG charts are encoded through _safe_chart — including the health trend, which uses the rolling-health series renamed to timestamp when available — and build_chart_specs produces the interactive ECharts counterparts, each chart failing independently.

sections.title: Narrative and gated NLP stages
sections.explanation: Tier A narrative (B2) runs unconditionally — pandas-only, never raises — then the gated stages run only when the probe said NLP is available. The emotion stage announces the model name and size before any from_pretrained (Pitfall 4), computes the summary over the scored sample when Option C sampling engaged, adds the emotion pie chart plus quarterly timeline spec, and degrades to None on failure. The narrative stage drives flan-t5-small over the signal digest and only accepts output passing the sanity gate; a failure keeps the Tier A observations. Finally the status block is stamped with the REAL gate state (B1) — no silent skips.

sections.title: Contract assembly and cache store
sections.explanation: adapters.adapt() maps everything into AnalysisResults, then a cache miss stores the result best-effort (never raising); on the NLP path with the cache disabled, a tip line advertises CHAT_ANALYZER_RESULT_CACHE=1 (D-06 hint pattern). The finally clause stops the progress bar even when a stage raised. This closes the orchestration loop: one function, one contract, every failure mode degraded rather than fatal.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/zip_input.py.overview: Support for the third input format: WhatsApp and Telegram 'Export chat' zips contain transcripts plus media, and this module turns such an archive into the same (rows, counts, source) contract the single-file parsers produce. It enumerates .txt/.json transcripts, counts the real media FILES in the archive so the report's media stat covers actual exports, lets the user pick transcripts interactively on a TTY, and merges every chosen transcript into one ParseReport-compatible result — so run_pipeline needs no changes downstream. Tour Step 7 pairs this file with pipeline.py as the zip branch of input detection.

sections.title: Module contract and design rules
sections.explanation: The docstring states the module's four jobs and the design rules it honors: reuse the existing hardened parsers (Item C — keep both formats, since Telegram never exports .txt), path-traversal-safe extraction (only the named member is read via zf.read and the extracted name is the member's basename), and never crash on a bad member (a failing transcript degrades to a warning while the others continue). Imports are minimal — tempfile, zipfile, pathlib, typer.

sections.title: Listing zip transcripts
sections.explanation: _list_transcripts scans the archive's namelist regardless of directory depth, skipping directory entries and classifying members by extension: .txt maps to the WhatsApp parser, .json to the Telegram parser. The lowercase comparison makes matching case-insensitive. It returns (member_name, kind) tuples — the raw inventory the selection step presents to the user.

sections.title: Counting archive media files
sections.explanation: count_zip_media_members counts every non-directory member that is not a transcript — the real jpg/mp4/opus/pdf files an 'Export chat' zip carries beside the text. The docstring warns this is a zip-LEVEL property: call it once per archive, never once per transcript, or the same files would be double-counted across merged transcripts. This count is what adapters.py later max-merges with the '<Media omitted>' marker count into the honest media_messages stat (D3/P17).

sections.title: Interactive transcript selection
sections.explanation: _select_transcripts never silently guesses: with multiple transcripts on a real terminal it lists them and asks for comma-separated numbers, validating picks in a loop with clear warnings. A single transcript skips the prompt entirely, and non-tty runs (piped/CI) fall back to analyzing ALL transcripts with a notice — the interactive/non-interactive duality used throughout the CLI. Pressing Enter with no input also selects everything.

sections.title: Safe member extraction and parse
sections.explanation: _parse_member reads exactly one named member with zf.read and writes its bytes to a temp file whose name is the member's basename — never the reconstructed archive path, closing the path-traversal hole. It then dispatches on kind: WhatsAppParser.parse_file_with_report for .txt members, the Telegram parse_telegram_chat_with_report for .json, returning the standard (rows, counts) shape. Parser imports happen inside the function so merely listing a zip never pays parser import cost.

sections.title: parse_zip_with_report merge
sections.explanation: The public entry point orchestrates: enumerate transcripts (raising a friendly ValueError on BadZipFile or no transcripts), let the user choose, then parse each chosen member inside a TemporaryDirectory. Counts are summed across transcripts, kinds are collected into a set to produce source 'whatsapp'/'telegram'/'mixed', and one failing transcript only warns and is skipped (Pitfall 6 degrade spirit). chosen_names lists ONLY successfully parsed transcripts, so a chosen-but-failed member rides the result-cache key without being misreported as analyzed. The zip-level media count is added once after the loop (D3/P17), and an empty merged row set still raises.

src/chat_analyzer/analysis/eda.py.overview: ChatEDA is the always-on exploratory analysis engine every install gets without any NLP download (tour Step 8). It enriches the canonical DataFrame in prepare_data with time features (day names, weekend flag, time period) and message features (word count, media marker, emoji detection), then computes three result families — message volume, conversation dynamics and content/vocabulary — that adapters.py and the comprehensive summary consume. The hot paths are vectorized, and generate_comprehensive_summary accepts precomputed results so pipeline.py can reuse them without recompute.

sections.title: Always-on imports
sections.explanation: The module's dependencies are the always-on stack only: itertools/re/Counter for tokenization, matplotlib for the dashboard stub, numpy and pandas for the analysis. No torch/transformers import appears — deliberate, since this module must import cleanly on a lean base install.

sections.title: prepare_data and time buckets
sections.explanation: __init__ copies the frame and immediately runs prepare_data, so every later analyzer works on enriched columns. prepare_data normalizes datetime/date, derives day-of-week names, weekday index, weekend flag and a Morning/Afternoon/Evening/Night time_period from the hour column, then adds message features: word_count via str.split, an is_media flag for '<Media omitted>' markers and a has_emoji regex over the emoji Unicode ranges. _categorize_time maps the 5-12/12-17/17-21/else boundaries — the day-part vocabulary the activity stats use.

sections.title: Message volume analysis
