sections.explanation: analyze_message_volume returns four grouped series in one dict: messages per day, a day-of-week x hour pivot matrix (the heatmap source), counts per time period and per-sender totals. The adapters use hourly_activity to find the busiest day and the pipeline feeds the same family of frames into the activity charts. Returning grouped pandas objects rather than scalars keeps one computation reusable by both the summary and the charts.

sections.title: Conversation dynamics
sections.explanation: The vectorized rewrite of the old loop-based dynamics: the frame is sorted by datetime, a sender-switch mask finds rows where the sender differs from the predecessor, and datetime.diff() gives the inter-message minutes — the response-time proxy. avg_response_time is None for chats with no switches (single-message edge case), and balance_ratio is min/max sender counts, a cheap participation balance. This is one of the module's parity-tested optimizations: the vectorized result must match a straightforward reference implementation.

sections.title: Content analysis
sections.explanation: analyze_content tokenizes vectorized: messages are lowercased, punctuation replaced by spaces, split, exploded, and tokens shorter than three characters dropped. A subtlety is preserved deliberately — Counter key order follows first occurrence in the token stream so ties in most_common break deterministically, which is why first_seen orders the Counter construction. Emoji frequency uses str.findall over the emoji ranges chained into one Counter. _clean_text remains as the per-message scalar cleaner the vectorized path replaced.

sections.title: Comprehensive summary
sections.explanation: generate_comprehensive_summary composes the three analyzers into the nested summary dict the pipeline passes to adapters: dataset_info (totals, participants, duration), activity_patterns (peak hour via idxmax and most active period), conversation_quality (balance and response time) and content_insights (word totals and emoji usage rate). Each sub-analysis can be passed in precomputed, which is exactly what run_pipeline does to avoid recompute. The summary is also stored on self for later reuse.

sections.title: Dashboard stub
sections.explanation: create_dashboard builds an empty 2x3 figure titled 'Chat Analysis Dashboard' — the comment admits the notebook visualization code was never ported, making this a template structure. The charts the CLI actually ships come from utils/visualization.ChatVisualizer instead, so this method is a vestigial extension point rather than a live code path.

src/chat_analyzer/analysis/sentiment.py.overview: The sentiment layer: VADER is the primary always-on engine, with optional TextBlob and an optional HuggingFace transformer backend that the CLI deliberately disables (pipeline.py pins TRANSFORMERS_AVAILABLE=False so a stray transformers install never loads a model on a base run). For huge chats, scoring fans out through a deduplication plus spawn-safe ProcessPoolExecutor path pinned at 2 workers — a measured optimum for the target hybrid CPU topology — with a deterministic sequential fallback. get_sentiment_summary produces the summary dict the adapter translates into the contract. Tour Step 8 covers this as the sentiment stage of the always-on engine.

sections.title: Availability flags and spawn guard
sections.explanation: The module probes optional dependencies at import: VADER and TextBlob import in try/except with availability flags, and _in_spawn_child suppresses child-side import noise (workers never touch TextBlob, NI-04). Crucially TRANSFORMERS_AVAILABLE is hardcoded False with a comment explaining the cost: a module-load transformers/torch import would cost 15-25 seconds and hundreds of MB for a CLI path that always runs VADER-only. This flag is the one pipeline.py flips off explicitly before importing, pinning the consensus to VADER.

sections.title: Config and analyzer initialization
sections.explanation: SentimentConfig holds the HF model name and the plus/minus 0.05 neutral thresholds. initialize_analyzers constructs the global VADER analyzer once, and only when the transformers flag were true would it build the HF pipeline with a try/except that degrades to VADER-only. The module-global singleton pattern matters for the parallel path below: workers must construct their own analyzers because the global is None in child processes.

sections.title: Per-message analyzer functions
sections.explanation: Three per-text scorers share one shape: guard on availability and empty/NaN text, then score. analyze_vader returns the polarity_scores dict; analyze_textblob adds polarity/subjectivity; analyze_huggingface truncates to 512 chars, maps HF labels into positive/negative/neutral, and degrades per-message failures to a neutral dict. These functions document the exact value contract the vectorized path must reproduce.

sections.title: Sentiment categorization
sections.explanation: categorize_sentiment maps a compound score onto Positive/Neutral/Negative using the plus/minus 0.05 thresholds from SentimentConfig, with optional per-call overrides. This is the bridge from continuous scores to the three-class distribution the report shows, and the same function labels both the VADER and TextBlob columns for the consensus vote.

sections.title: Parallel VADER scoring
sections.explanation: The optimization core: _score_vader_parallel deduplicates scorable strings (polarity_scores is a pure function of the string), short-circuits empty rows to the neutral dict, and above the 20,000-message threshold fans unique strings out to a ProcessPoolExecutor in 10,000-item chunks. Worker count is pinned at 2 with a measured rationale (ME-02): on the 2P+8E target laptop only the two P-cores scale (1.97x, 99% efficiency); more workers land on E-cores and add spawn/IPC churn. _vader_score_batch constructs a worker-LOCAL analyzer because the module global is None in spawn children, and the HI-01 branch preserves the all-neutral fallback when initialization was skipped; any pool failure degrades to sequential scoring, and output order is restored from the original key list.

sections.title: add_sentiment_analysis
sections.explanation: The DataFrame-level entry point: copies the frame, runs VADER through the parallel helper, spreads the four VADER columns plus the categorized label, optionally runs TextBlob and the HF path, then computes consensus_sentiment as the majority vote across whichever analyzers ran (a single analyzer degrades to that label directly). The prints narrate progress — which is why the pipeline wraps this call in redirect_stdout. The returned frame is what get_sentiment_summary and the sentiment charts consume.

sections.title: Sentiment summary
sections.explanation: get_sentiment_summary builds the four-part summary dict: total count, the consensus distribution, average VADER/TextBlob score stats (mean/std/min/max), per-sender breakdowns with counts and average scores, and temporal analysis (daily and hourly average compound). The adapter reads exactly these keys — sentiment_distribution, average_scores.vader_compound.mean, by_sender and temporal_analysis.daily_avg_sentiment — so this dict's shape is the module's public contract.

sections.title: Dashboards and extremes
sections.explanation: plot_sentiment_analysis renders a 2x2 matplotlib dashboard (distribution pie, daily timeline with a zero baseline, per-sender bars, hourly bars color-coded by tone) and ends in plt.show — the interactive-notebook pattern that returns None and therefore cannot feed the HTML report's base64 embedding, which is why the CLI uses ChatVisualizer's figure-returning variants instead. find_extreme_messages picks the n most positive and negative messages by VADER compound with sender and score attached — a utility for future report features.

sections.title: Quick analysis entry point
sections.explanation: quick_sentiment_analysis chains add_sentiment_analysis + get_sentiment_summary + optional plotting — the notebook-era convenience API. The __main__ block prints module usage, reinforcing that this file is a library module, not a script. The CLI itself uses only the first two functions, pinned to the VADER tier.

src/chat_analyzer/analysis/relationship_.overview: The largest always-on analysis module: it scores conversation health from measurable patterns — who starts conversations (a 60-minute gap or calendar-day rule), how fast each side responds, and who dominates (message count, length, conversation control, bursts) — combining them into a weighted overall health score with grades. A rolling-window tracker re-scores health over a 7-day sliding window using an incremental fast path that is parity-tested against the original per-window recompute; gamification features add a Friendship Index, streaks, milestones and emoji personalities; matplotlib dashboards round it out. analyze_relationship_health is the pipeline's single entry point, returning everything including the prepared_data DataFrame that must never leak into the report. Tour Step 8 covers this as one of the five always-on engine modules.

sections.title: Module header and logging
sections.explanation: The docstring enumerates the module's feature history: initiator ratio, response lag, dominance, health scoring, the Day 9 rolling tracker, Day 14 gamification and Day 13 visualization integration. The logging setup attaches a NullHandler — Anti-Pattern 4: never hijack global log config at import — so library code stays configurable by the host. Imports are the always-on stack: matplotlib, numpy, pandas.

sections.title: Starters and initiator ratio
sections.explanation: identify_conversation_starters sorts by datetime and marks a row as a starter when the inter-message gap exceeds 60 minutes OR the calendar day changed — with a subtle vectorized edge-case note: row 0's NaN gap compares False, but its date comparison against the shifted NaT is True, and it is force-marked anyway. calculate_initiator_ratio then counts starters per sender, computes a balance score (1 minus the gap between the two top initiators over total conversations) and maps it through a four-step interpretation ladder. A chat with no starters returns an error dict rather than raising.

sections.title: Response patterns and dominance
sections.explanation: analyze_response_patterns filters non-starter rows with a different sender and a valid gap — the vectorized equivalent of the old iterrows loop, preserving row order — and aggregates per-responder statistics plus who-responds-to-whom pairs; responsiveness and balance scores normalize against 120-minute-slow and 60-minute-imbalance anchors. calculate_dominance_scores blends four balance measures: message counts, total character lengths, conversation control (who sends the last message before the next starter) and burst patterns via run-length encoding of consecutive same-sender messages. The composite dominance score averages the first three and maps onto an interpretation ladder.

sections.title: Overall health score
sections.explanation: calculate_relationship_health_score combines the three metric dicts with fixed weights — responsiveness 0.35 (deliberately the most important), initiation 0.25, response balance and dominance 0.20 each — into an overall 0-1 score. Grade bands run EXCELLENT at 0.90 down to NEEDS IMPROVEMENT below 0.60, and the component scores generate strengths vs areas-for-improvement lists with emoji markers. This is the score the adapters surface as overall_score and grade, and the lead-in the report qualifies as speculative, not a verdict.

sections.title: Rolling health reference path
sections.explanation: The rolling tracker's constants encode a performance decision: _ROLLING_PARALLEL_MIN_DATES is set to 2^62 so production ALWAYS takes the incremental path, while the process-pool branch is retained purely as the reference/verification path that parity tests force by lowering the threshold. _rolling_window_score is the gold standard — a full per-window recompute running the unmodified metric functions. _date_row_spans precomputes each date's [start, stop) row offsets in the date-sorted frame, which the fast path slices instead of rebuilding windows by concat.

sections.title: Rolling health fast path
sections.explanation: _rolling_window_fast reproduces the reference math bit-for-bit from columns computed ONCE over the full frame, skipping the redundant per-window identify pass and the dead aggregations; its long docstring argues why the starter/diff/prev columns are window-invariant (each window's first row is already marked a starter by the day-change rule). calculate_rolling_health_score sorts dates, optionally runs the forced-parallel reference, then walks the sliding window with a moving lower index — each window is a positional slice scored by the fast function. Windows below min_messages are skipped and failing windows log a warning instead of crashing the series.

sections.title: Friendship Index and streaks
sections.explanation: calculate_friendship_index is the gamified composite: communication frequency (0-25, capped at 50 messages/day), initiator balance (0-25), responsiveness (0-20), engagement quality via average message length (0-15, capped at 100 chars) and consistency via the longest streak (0-15, capped at 30 days), summed to 0-100 and mapped onto five emoji tiers from ACQUAINTANCES to BEST FRIENDS. detect_conversation_streaks walks the sorted unique dates counting consecutive-day runs, and checks the current streak against the real-world today — deliberately naive local-calendar semantics (noqa DTZ005).

sections.title: Emoji personality and milestones
sections.explanation: analyze_emoji_personality extracts emojis per sender with a broad Unicode regex, categorizes them into positive/negative/neutral/excited/laughing buckets, and maps the dominant category onto personality types (Optimist, Comedian, Enthusiast and so on) with traits and a usage level from the per-message emoji rate. detect_milestones turns totals into achievements: message-count thresholds (100 to 50000), day thresholds (7 to 730), streaks of 7 days or more, and special badges (Night Owl after 11 PM, Early Bird before 6 AM, Weekend Warrior above 30 percent weekend share), each with an icon and progress toward the next milestone.

sections.title: Matplotlib dashboards
sections.explanation: The dashboard layer: plot_relationship_health_dashboard_enhanced builds a 3x3 gridspec (health trend line, friendship gauge drawn with polar wedges, streak/emoji/achievement text panels, component bars), preferring the visualization module and falling back to _plot_original_dashboard with its gauge, radar chart and per-metric panels. All of these end in plt.show() and return None — which is exactly why the pipeline cannot use them for HTML embedding and relies on ChatVisualizer's figure-returning health-trend plot instead.

sections.title: analyze_relationship_health entry point
sections.explanation: The single pipeline-facing function: prepare starters, compute the three metric families, calculate the health score, then optionally attach gamification (friendship index, streaks, milestones, emoji personality) and the rolling series — pipeline.py calls it with include_gamification=False since only the rolling_health DataFrame feeds the health trend chart. The result dict carries everything including prepared_data, which adapters.py explicitly refuses to copy into the contract. example_usage and the __main__ block demonstrate the full call for interactive exploration.

src/chat_analyzer/analysis/network_graph.overview: Builds a directed sender-to-sender reply graph — an edge A to B is created each time B sends a message right after A — then layers metrics on top: density, degree/in-degree/out-degree/betweenness centralities, PageRank, connectivity and diameter. identify_key_participants maps those metrics onto social roles (most active, most responsive, most influential, bridge connector), interaction patterns extract the strongest connections and reciprocity, and community detection uses greedy modularity with a connected-components fallback. network_figure is the small figure-returning wrapper the pipeline embeds as base64, since the plot helpers themselves end in plt.show(). Tour Step 8 covers this as one of the five always-on engine modules.

sections.title: Module header and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring scopes the module: reply networks, interaction frequencies, centrality, community detection — designed for group chats of 3+ participants but working at any size. Imports bring networkx, pandas, matplotlib and seaborn (the last used only by the dashboard heatmap). Nothing NLP-related appears here — this module is part of the tier every install gets.

sections.title: Building the interaction network
sections.explanation: build_interaction_network sorts messages by time and builds the DiGraph vectorized: a sender-switch mask finds consecutive-message handoffs, and a groupby over (previous sender, current sender) counts each directed pair. Every participant becomes a node even without edges, and edges below weight_threshold are dropped. This consecutive-message proxy for replying is the module's core modeling decision — cheap, deterministic, and honest for turn-taking chats.

sections.title: Network metrics
sections.explanation: calculate_network_metrics computes the descriptive layer: node/edge counts and density, three degree centralities, betweenness (only for weakly connected graphs, else empty — it can fail on disconnected graphs), PageRank (works on any graph), and connectivity flags with the undirected diameter. The try/except around the centralities degrades optional metrics to empty dicts rather than crashing the run. These metrics are what adapters extract into the serializable network block.

sections.title: Key participant roles
sections.explanation: identify_key_participants translates each metric's argmax into a social role: most_active (out-degree — initiates the most handoffs), most_responsive (in-degree — receives the most), most_influential (PageRank) and bridge_connector (betweenness — sits on the most shortest paths). Each role carries the participant and the raw score. Guarding every metric's presence keeps the function honest on tiny or disconnected graphs where some metrics are empty.

sections.title: Interaction patterns
sections.explanation: analyze_interaction_patterns sorts edges by weight into the top-5 strongest_connections list, pairs reciprocal edges (A to B and B to A both present) with a balance ratio, and computes a reciprocity score — the share of reciprocal pairs among half the edge count. The interaction matrix DataFrame (who talks to whom) is built for the dashboard heatmap. Note for two-person chats: both directions of every switch are reciprocal and tied, which adapters.py later disarms with its tie-aware summary wording.

sections.title: Community detection
sections.explanation: detect_subgroups converts to undirected and runs greedy_modularity_communities (Louvain-style, best modularity) inside a try/except whose fallback is plain connected components with modularity None. This guards against the optional python-louvain dependency being absent. The subgroup count is all the report shows — adapters extract only len(subgroups).

sections.title: Network plot function
sections.explanation: plot_network_graph draws the graph with a choice of layouts (spring seeded at 42 for reproducibility, circular, kamada_kawai), node sizes from a chosen metric, edge widths proportional to weights, and red weight labels. It ends with plt.show() — the interactive-notebook pattern that returns None and therefore cannot be embedded into the HTML report. It remains useful for notebooks and manual exploration.

sections.title: Network dashboard
sections.explanation: plot_network_dashboard composes a 3x3 gridspec: the main graph, PageRank bars, degree bars, the interaction-matrix heatmap (seaborn) and a monospace statistics text panel including the strongest connection. Like the other plot helpers it calls plt.show() and returns nothing — the pipeline instead uses network_figure for its single embeddable chart.

sections.title: analyze_network and network_figure
sections.explanation: analyze_network is the complete pipeline the CLI calls: build, metrics, key participants, patterns, subgroups — returning the graph itself alongside the dicts (the DiGraph is intentionally included; adapters.py is the component that strips it out). network_figure is the integration shim (Pattern 2/Pitfall 6): the module's own plot helpers end in plt.show() and return None, so this thin wrapper draws with a seeded spring layout, does NOT show, and returns the figure for pipeline.fig_to_data_uri to base64-embed — consuming the already-computed result rather than re-running the analysis.

sections.title: Example usage
sections.explanation: example_usage fabricates a tiny 3-participant frame, runs analyze_network, prints the headline metrics and opens the dashboard — a self-demo for manual testing, mirroring the pattern in relationship_health.py. The __main__ guard keeps it inert on import.

src/chat_analyzer/analysis/narrative.py.overview: Tier A of the two-tier narrative system: the always-on, heuristic 'what is going on' layer built on pandas and re only — never importing from cli, never touching torch/transformers. It turns chat signals into clearly-disclaimed, hedged observations (arc from casual chat toward planning, question-driven conversation drivers, sensitive-topic drivers, turn-taking reciprocity, message-length engagement) plus one factual snapshot baseline that is never hedged. Every claim is speculative by design, confidence comes from a conservative threshold table, and analyze_narrative never raises — edge cases degrade to the base dict. Tour Step 8 positions this as the narrative tier every install gets.

sections.title: Tier A contract and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring defines the tier boundary precisely: Tier A is pandas plus re, imports nothing from chat_analyzer.cli, and its status block always reports that only Tier A ran (Tier B fills it later in pipeline.py). Observation kinds form a small stable vocabulary — snapshot, arc, driver, reciprocity and engagement emitted here; sentiment and visibility reserved for Tier B. Every text must be ASCII-only and hedged, with the snapshot as the sole factual exception.

sections.title: Lexicons and compiled patterns
sections.explanation: Three Banglish keyword lexicons (care/trust, planning, question words) are combined with English equivalents into three compiled regexes with word-boundary anchors and IGNORECASE. Whole-token matching matters: 'ki' must not match inside other words. These compiled patterns are reused by the question-ratio, topic-driver and arc-signal extractors, so lexicon changes propagate everywhere consistently.

sections.title: Safety normalizers
sections.explanation: _ascii_safe strips non-ASCII characters from sender names and falls back to 'one participant' — guaranteeing report-safe output for non-Latin names. _normalize copies the frame, renames NaN senders to 'unknown', coerces messages to str and guarantees a numeric message_length column exists. These two helpers are why the module can claim analyze_narrative never raises on messy input.

sections.title: Confidence and length asymmetry
sections.explanation: _confidence is the documented conservative table: high needs 30 or more messages AND a signal magnitude of 0.5, medium needs 10 AND 0.3, anything else low — so weak signals never sound authoritative. _message_length_asymmetry compares the mean message length of the two most active senders, returning a ratio of at least 1.0 plus which side writes longer, or an empty dict when no pairwise comparison is possible. The ratio feeds the engagement observation when it clears 2.5x.

sections.title: Question ratio and reciprocity
sections.explanation: _question_ratio_per_sender flags messages containing a question mark or an English wh-word/Banglish marker, computes per-sender ratios, and only emits the much-more driver flag when the leader clears 0.4 AND beats second place by 0.25 with both sides having at least 2 messages — a deliberately strict bar. _reciprocity measures turn-taking as the share of adjacent sender pairs that change: near 1.0 for balanced back-and-forth, near 0 for stacked monologues. Both return rich dicts so callers can attach confidence.

sections.title: Topic driver and arc signal
sections.explanation: _sensitive_topic_driver counts per-sender hits of the care/trust (sensitive) and planning lexicons, computes topic density per sender, and names a leader only when their density lead clears 0.3 with at least one topic message. _arc_signal splits the chat at its midpoint and keeps an arc only when the later half is clearly denser in topic-loaded messages (later density above 0.2, delta at least 0.2, at least 4 total hits) — the observation that the conversation possibly shifts from casual chat toward planning/decision. Both guards prevent one-off mentions from creating a narrative.

sections.title: Snapshot and observation builder
sections.explanation: _snapshot_observation is the always-present factual baseline (WS-6): total messages, participants, days and the top sender's share — never hedged, confidence high. _build_observations then appends hedged observations only when each extractor's strict threshold passes: arc, question-driven driver, sensitive-topic driver, one-sided reciprocity (below 0.45 with 4 or more alternating pairs) and long-message engagement (ratio 2.5x or more). The override helper lets Tier B inject precomputed signals instead of recomputation. Every observation text begins with a hedge and carries a kind and confidence.

sections.title: analyze_narrative entry point
sections.explanation: The public function validates shape first (empty frame, missing columns, fewer than 2 senders or 2 messages all return the base dict with empty observations — never raising), normalizes, then builds observations inside a blanket try/except so analysis can never crash the run. narrative_summary is simply the observation texts joined — the same content the Tier B digest later consumes. The returned dict matches the contract shape adapters.py normalizes, with tier A and speculative True.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/nlp_gate.py.overview: The checkpoint that decides whether the heavy NLP tier can run at all. nlp_available is a silent importability probe — transformers and torch importable, never raising, never prompting — with the CHAT_ANALYZER_FORCE_NLP env override making both branches deterministic in tests. The module also holds the locked model constants (DistilBERT emotion ~255 MB, flan-t5-small ~340 MB), the environment knobs (emotion sample cap, worker count, result cache dir), the tier status resolution used by the interactive menu, and the guarded runtime installer with the Windows MAX_PATH guard that points at scripts/make_nlp_env.ps1. Tour Step 9 walks this file as the gate that keeps the heavy tier lazy.

sections.title: Gate philosophy and constants
sections.explanation: The docstring states the D-01/D-02 doctrine: the pipeline always PREPARES for NLP, but the heavy models only run when this pure probe says the packages import — failures resolve to False with no prompt and no hint (that is main.py's job). Model weights are NOT required up front; they download on first use, fixing the first-install gap for fresh [nlp] installs. The locked constants follow: both model IDs with announced sizes, the four environment-variable names, and the Windows MAX_PATH arithmetic (260-char limit, 180-char torch reserve) that backs the long-path guard.

sections.title: Model cache and sample cap
sections.explanation: model_cached checks the huggingface_hub canonical cache (falling back to the home .cache/huggingface/hub path) for the models--<id> directory — the flag the pipeline prints its 'Downloading model weights on first run' notice from. emotion_sample_cap resolves CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_SAMPLE with whitelist semantics: absent means the default 50000, '0'/'off'/'false' or any value parsing to non-positive means None (always exact), positive integers are honored, and garbage falls back to the default. Returning None is the pipeline's signal to skip sampling entirely.

sections.title: Worker count and cache dir knobs
sections.explanation: emotion_worker_count mirrors the cap's semantics for CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_WORKERS: '0'/'1'/'off'/'false' or anything parsing below 2 means sequential; otherwise the value is capped at min(requested, cpu_count, 8) because each worker loads its own ~255 MB model copy. result_cache_enabled and result_cache_dir resolve CHAT_ANALYZER_RESULT_CACHE: off-words disable, on-words pick the OS default (%LOCALAPPDATA%\chat-analyzer\cache on Windows, ~/.cache/chat-analyzer elsewhere), and any other value IS the directory verbatim. The dir resolution is side-effect-free — no mkdir here — because directory creation belongs to store().

sections.title: Availability probe and version pins
sections.explanation: nlp_available tries importing torch and transformers — nothing more; cached weights no longer gate availability, which is the first-install-gap fix. CHAT_ANALYZER_FORCE_NLP wins when set, making tests deterministic on a dev machine where transformers exists but no model is cached (RESEARCH Pitfall 5). The [nlp] extras pins are mirrored from pyproject.toml with a do-not-drift warning, and nlp_installed_versions/nlp_versions_satisfied report per-package presence and pin satisfaction for the tier menu.

sections.title: Tier status resolution
sections.explanation: nlp_status collapses the environment into MISSING (a package absent), OUTDATED (installed but outside the pins, or weights not cached) or READY (pins satisfied and both models cached), returning a detail dict with the underlying versions for the CLI to display. This is the tier-2/3 resolution the interactive menu consults before offering the NLP path. The distinction matters: OUTDATED is fixable by update_nlp plus download_models without touching the package set.

sections.title: Guarded pip installer
sections.explanation: _pip_install runs pip as a subprocess with captured output and a 900-second timeout — a multi-GB download must never echo forever or hang the terminal (WR-02). Timeout and nonzero exit both raise the same friendly RuntimeError so callers degrade to basic analysis plus the hint line. Using sys.executable -m pip avoids shell injection entirely (T-04-10: never shell=True).

sections.title: Windows long-path guard
sections.explanation: registry_long_paths_enabled reads the LongPathsEnabled registry DWORD — when the user enabled long paths system-wide, the guard must not warn. windows_long_path_message then checks the CHAT_ANALYZER_ALLOW_LONG_PATH override and measures whether the venv's site-packages path plus the 180-char torch reserve fits under 260 chars; if not, it returns an instructive remediation message naming scripts/make_nlp_env.ps1 and the short-path fix under %TEMP%. The reserve is heuristic — hence the override — and the check prevents a multi-GB download from crashing with WinError 206 before it starts.

sections.title: Install, update, download
sections.explanation: install_nlp and update_nlp are the D-05 runtime paths: both run the long-path guard first, then pip-install the already-declared [nlp] extras (no new dependency names enter the graph). The CPU-only split exists because --index-url REPLACES PyPI — torch must come from the PyTorch CPU index while transformers is installed separately from PyPI (WR-01). download_models snapshot-downloads BOTH locked weight sets into the HF cache, making tier selection the consent point, and raises RuntimeError on failure so the caller degrades to basic analysis.

scripts/make_nlp_env.ps1.overview: The concrete workaround behind the NLP gate's Windows long-path warning: a PowerShell helper that creates a disposable NLP venv at a short path (default: TEMP) and installs the project with its [nlp] extras into it. Deep venv paths crash pip install torch on Windows with WinError 206, so CI and stage D1 call this helper to prepare the NLP environment at, for example, %TEMP%\chat-analyzer-nlp — a path far under the 260-character limit. Tour Step 9 pairs it with nlp_gate.windows_long_path_message, whose remediation text names this script.

sections.title: Parameters and cleanup
sections.explanation: The header comment states the why (WinError 206 on deep paths) and who calls it (CI / stage D1). param takes an optional BasePath defaulting to the TEMP environment variable, $ErrorActionPreference Stop makes any native failure abort, and the venv directory is chat-analyzer-nlp under that base. An existing env is removed recursively first — the disposable, idempotent-rerun philosophy: recreating the environment is always safe.

sections.title: Venv creation and extras install
sections.explanation: The py launcher creates the venv with an explicit exit-code check and throw (Python failures do not raise PowerShell exceptions), then the venv's own python upgrades pip and pip-installs the project editable WITH the [nlp] extras, where projectRoot is derived from the script's own location. The try/catch prints the failure message and exits 1 rather than leaving a half-built env silently appearing to succeed. Installing torch here is exactly the operation that would crash from a deep path, which is the whole point of the short location.

sections.title: Activation instructions
sections.explanation: The final step prints how to activate the env (Scripts\Activate.ps1) and run the analyzer inside it — the user-facing contract of the helper. Because the env lives under TEMP, it is disposable: deleting it never touches the project or a persistent Python installation.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/result_cache.py.overview: The opt-in disk cache that makes repeat runs of an unchanged chat take seconds instead of minutes or hours (tour Step 9). The full AnalysisResults payload is persisted as JSON under a user-local directory keyed by sha256 of the input file bytes plus a config signature (app version, NLP on/off, sample cap, worker count, chosen zip transcripts) — so any change to inputs or configuration produces a new key. The privacy contract is explicit: only derived data is cached (never raw chat text), the directory lives outside the repo, loading uses json only (never pickle/eval), corrupt entries self-heal, and stale entries are pruned on a 30-day TTL.

sections.title: Privacy contract and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring is the security spec: cache outside the repo tree (the default dirs resolved by nlp_gate), payload is derived data only, JSON-only loading, and key filenames are hex digests so no user input ever enters a path. numpy is an optional import guarded so the module loads in non-numpy environments. The TTL constant (30 days) and the 1 MiB hash chunk size are defined up front — hashing a 20 MB file takes roughly 0.1-0.3 seconds.

sections.title: File hash and app version
sections.explanation: sha256_file reads the file in 1 MiB chunks and hashes raw bytes — deliberately ignoring mtime/size, so a touch on the input still hits the cache, and zip inputs hash the WHOLE archive bytes including media members. _app_version returns the installed package version or 'dev' for editable installs, guarded against PackageNotFoundError. Both fold into the cache key so app upgrades invalidate.

sections.title: Cache key composition
sections.explanation: cache_key builds the deterministic key: sha256 of a sort_keys JSON payload combining the file digest with the config signature {schema, app_version, nlp_on, sample_cap, emotion_workers, chosen_transcripts (sorted)}. Sorting makes the signature byte-stable regardless of dict construction order. The returned hex digest becomes the filename <key>.json — the reason path traversal is impossible by construction.

sections.title: Payload sanitizer
sections.explanation: _sanitize recursively coerces the results dict to JSON-safe plain data: numpy scalars become native Python (ndarrays via tolist), non-finite floats (NaN/Inf) become None, and dict keys that are not JSON-native — the verified leak being sentiment's daily_avg keyed by datetime.date — become their str() form. The numpy checks are guarded on the optional import so the walk never crashes without numpy. This is what makes storing AnalysisResults safe despite its pandas-derived contents.

sections.title: load
sections.explanation: load reads the <key>.json entry with json.loads only — never pickle/eval (T-04-20). A corrupt file is deleted (self-healing so the next run re-analyzes), while a schema mismatch or wrong-shaped payload returns None but is NOT deleted (a newer-format file stays for a future version). report_path is always blanked on load (Q2.4) because main.py fills it fresh after writing the current report. Every failure path returns None — the cache can never break a run.

sections.title: store and TTL prune
sections.explanation: store writes the envelope {schema, app_version, created_at (UTC ISO-8601), sanitized results} through a same-directory temp file and os.replace — atomic on the same volume and Windows-safe, giving last-write-wins for concurrent runs of the same file (Q5.6). _prune runs on every store, deleting .json entries older than 30 days by mtime, best-effort per entry. Any failure anywhere is logged and swallowed: the pipeline never crashes because of the cache.

src/chat_analyzer/analysis/emotion.py.overview: One of the two NLP-tier heavyweights unlocked by the gate from Step 9: a HuggingFace DistilBERT text-classification pipeline that scores every message across six fixed emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, love). To scale to huge chats it offers a deterministic stratified sample above a 50,000-message cap, process-pool parallel exact scoring for large unique-text sets, and an opt-in INT8 quantization knob. The pipeline stage consumes `analyze_emotions`' enriched DataFrame and the summary getters, whose output feeds both the terminal report and the HTML chart specs.

sections.title: Module docstring and sampled-path contract
sections.explanation: The docstring doubles as the design contract. It names the six emotions, the heavy dependencies (transformers, torch), and the usage pattern, then specifies the 'Option C' sampled path in detail: when more scorable messages exist than `sample_cap` (default 50,000), a DETERMINISTIC stratified sample is scored instead — seats allocated across senders by largest remainder, then across ~50 time buckets, all with `random_state=42` so the same frame plus cap always yields the same sample. Non-selected rows keep neutral 1/6 scores, the frame gains an `emotion_scored` column and `df.attrs['emotion_sample']` metadata, and below the cap behavior is byte-for-byte the exact path. The reproducibility promise is the key idea: sampling is a pure function of the data.

sections.title: Imports, singletons, and constants
sections.explanation: Module-level `_emotion_analyzer` / `_emotion_model_loaded` are singletons so a second `EmotionAnalyzer` instance reuses the already-loaded pipeline instead of paying the model-load cost again. `EMOTION_LABELS` is the single source of truth — the fixed column order for `emotion_*` columns, the keys of every score dict, and the model's label order with `top_k=None`. The tuning constants matter: `_EMOTION_SAMPLE_RNG = 42` plus `_TIME_BUCKETS = 50` parameterize the deterministic sample, `_EMOTION_PARALLEL_THRESHOLD = 20_000` keeps small chats fully sequential (byte-identical output, no spawn churn), and `_MIN_CHUNK_TEXTS = 512` sizes bounded work chunks for the pool.

sections.title: Spawn worker and opt-in INT8 quantization
sections.explanation: `_score_text_chunk` is the `ProcessPoolExecutor` entry point, and it follows the Windows-spawn rule: module-level, taking ONLY JSON-able arguments, with the heavy pipeline constructed INSIDE the child and torch threads clamped to `cpu_count // workers` so the pool never oversubscribes the machine. Two gotchas are documented inline: `truncation=True` is mandatory because a ≤512-CHAR message can still exceed the model's 512-TOKEN position budget (emoji/CJK-dense text used to hard-crash DistilBERT), and a failing batch degrades to per-message scoring then neutral scores so one bad batch never loses its chunk. `_maybe_quantize_pipeline` applies dynamic qint8 quantization only when `CHAT_ANALYZER_EMOTION_QUANT` is truthy — default OFF because measurements showed ~1.7x throughput but dominant-label agreement dropping to ~75% with systematic surprise/love→joy flips.

sections.title: Deterministic stratified sampling helpers
sections.explanation: This block implements the reproducible sample. `_allocate_seats` is largest-remainder allocation — every sender keeps at least one seat when the cap permits, leftovers refill round-robin by largest fractional remainder (tie-broken by name), allocations never exceed a sender's count, and the result is a pure function of (counts, cap). `_pick_in_sender` then stratifies one sender's rows across ~50 qcut time buckets with `random_state=42` draws, degrading through global bucket edges to a plain sample; the CR-01 comment is worth reading — qcut can silently succeed with ALL-NaN buckets when timestamps collapse to one unique value, which would drop that sender to zero rows without the explicit `notna` check. `_stratified_sample_indices` ties it together, returning a boolean mask with exactly `min(cap, n_scorable)` True entries plus a defensive top-up that guarantees the count contract.

sections.title: Score normalization, model init, and batch scoring
sections.explanation: `_parse_emotion_scores` normalizes two transformers shapes into one standard dict: 4.x returns a flat list of `{label, score}` dicts with `top_k=None`, while 5.x nests it one level deeper — the code unwraps the nested form and defaults missing labels to 0.0, shared by parent and worker so every path parses identically. `EmotionAnalyzer.__init__` pins the model id (`bhadresh-savani/distilbert-base-uncased-emotion`) and `_initialize_model` reuses the module singleton, building `pipeline('text-classification', top_k=None, device=-1)` with a rule-based fallback on load failure (D-17: never crash). `analyze_single_message` short-circuits empty, media-marker, and <3-char messages to neutral scores; `_is_scorable` mirrors that gate exactly so the sampling decision and the analyzer agree on what gets scored (IN-01); `_score_batch` scores in chunks with the same degrade-to-per-message contract — note the deliberately ASCII-safe error print, because an emoji there crashed cp1252 consoles inside the error handler.

sections.title: Deduplicated process-pool parallel scoring
sections.explanation: Emotion scoring is a pure function of the text, so `_score_unique_texts` first dedupes with `dict.fromkeys` and scores every UNIQUE text once, mapping results back — output stays byte-identical to per-row scoring. Parallelism is triple-gated: a REAL `transformers.Pipeline` instance (`_is_real_pipeline` deliberately keeps pytest mocks sequential since a mock is neither picklable nor pipeline-backed), a validated worker count ≥2 (`_scoring_workers` clamps like nlp_gate: `max(1, min(value, cpu_count, 8))`), and more than 20,000 unique texts. `_score_unique_texts_parallel` then splits into bounded contiguous chunks (several per worker so idle cores pull the next chunk), consumes results as they complete, keeps every completed chunk, and re-scores only lost slices in the parent — the fix for the measured pathology where one spawn child dying at teardown threw away all completed work for a full sequential re-run. If nothing comes back, `None` degrades to the caller's sequential fallback.

sections.title: Neutral scores, vectorized write-back, fallback
sections.explanation: Three support pieces. `_get_neutral_emotions` returns uniform 1/6 scores — the value unselected rows keep in sampled mode. `_write_emotion_columns` replaces a per-row `.at` write loop with one numpy matrix materialization followed by one column assignment per emotion, roughly an order of magnitude faster on 400k+ rows, writing positionally over the parser's guaranteed-unique RangeIndex. `_rule_based_emotion` is the no-model fallback: keyword plus emoji counts per emotion, normalized into a distribution (or neutral scores when nothing matched) — it keeps the module usable when transformers is absent or failed to load.

sections.title: analyze_emotions orchestration
sections.explanation: The main entry point, and the place the sampled/exact/fallback branches meet. It copies the frame, initializes the six `emotion_*` columns to 0.0, then branches three ways. Sampled path (cap exceeded): select the deterministic sample, score only those rows through the same dedupe/batch path, give every other row neutral scores, and stamp `emotion_scored` plus the `df.attrs['emotion_sample']` dict. Exact path: score all scorable rows; if the sampling machinery failed but exact scoring ran anyway, the attrs still record the honest failure note so the pipeline labels the report correctly. No-model path: the unchanged per-message rule-based loop. Finally, `dominant_emotion` (idxmax over the emotion columns) and `emotion_confidence` (the max) are computed over the FULL frame, not just the sample.

sections.title: Summaries, top messages, and timeline
sections.explanation: The read-side getters the pipeline consumes. `get_emotion_summary` builds the report block: the `dominant_emotion` value counts, per-emotion averages plus an intensity block (mean/std/max/min), per-sender statistics when a `sender` column exists, and a by-date dominant-emotion grouping when `datetime` exists. `find_most_emotional_messages` returns the top-n rows for one specific emotion or by overall confidence; `get_emotion_timeline` returns per-date mean emotion scores. The `get_emotion_quarterly` method here is a thin wrapper delegating to the module-level function — the contract that `chart_json.build_emotion_timeline_spec` consumes for the report's quarterly chart.

sections.title: Quarterly contract, quick API, and plotting
sections.explanation: The module-level `get_emotion_quarterly` is the serialization contract for the report: `[{'quarter': '2026Q1', 'scores': {...}}]` — per-quarter means of the six emotion columns, oldest first, rounded to 6 decimals, aggregating only `emotion_scored` rows when the frame is in sampled mode so chart values and report labels agree, and never raising (empty/missing-datetime frames yield `[]`). `quick_emotion_analysis` is the one-call convenience; `plot_emotion_analysis` draws the interactive 2x2 matplotlib dashboard; `emotion_figure` is the report variant that RETURNS the Figure with no `plt.show()` so the pipeline's `_safe_chart` can base64-encode it; `combine_sentiment_emotion` merges sentiment and emotion columns by index.

src/chat_analyzer/analysis/summarizer.py.overview: The NLP tier's second heavyweight: T5-small abstractive conversation summarization with group-chat support. `ConversationSummarizer` can summarize a whole conversation, a date range, a single participant, or periodic windows, and layers extractive group analysis on top — group-type detection, dominant-speaker ranking, consecutive-turn interaction counting, and key-topic extraction. The pipeline's Tier B stage drives it when the nlp_gate confirms the model is available; generation runs through T5's conditional `generate()` directly because transformers 5.x removed the `summarization` pipeline task.

sections.title: Module docstring and imports
sections.explanation: A compact header announcing the module's role: conversation summarization using the T5-small transformer, enhanced with group-chat analysis features. Imports stay deliberately light — `pandas`, `warnings`, and `collections.Counter` — because the heavy transformers imports are deferred into `__init__`, keeping the module importable (and testable with mocks) even without the NLP extra installed.

sections.title: Class init and direct T5 load
sections.explanation: The constructor takes the model name (`t5-small`), the summary length window (`max_length=150` / `min_length=40`), and `max_participants_in_report` — the knob that caps how many per-participant summaries a large group produces. The key design note is in the comment: the abstractive summary runs through `model.generate()` directly, NOT `pipeline('summarization', ...)`, because transformers 5.x removed that pipeline task and the direct call works across 4.x and 5.x alike. Unlike the emotion module's rule-based fallback, a failed load here re-raises — Tier B is all-or-nothing by design.

sections.title: _prepare_text: token-budget digest
sections.explanation: The pragmatic bridge between a potentially huge chat and T5-small's 512-token encoder limit: take at most the first 100 messages, format each as `sender: message`, skip empty rows and `<Media omitted>` markers, join with spaces, then hard-truncate the whole string at 2,000 characters. This is a head-of-conversation digest, not a map-reduce summary — worth noticing because it means the summary reflects the chat's opening stretch, a deliberate simplicity trade-off.

sections.title: Group type detection
sections.explanation: `detect_group_type` counts distinct senders and buckets the chat: 1-on-1 (≤2), Small (≤5), Medium (≤15), Large (>15), returning the type, participant count, a human description, and total messages. Cheap pandas work that gives the report and `analyze_group_dynamics` a one-line framing of the conversation's shape.

sections.title: Interaction matrix
sections.explanation: Builds the sender→receiver turn-taking matrix: for every ordered pair, it counts how many times one participant's message is immediately followed by the other's, using positional index adjacency (`idx + 1`). The O(N·P²) nested loop is the straightforward reference implementation — readable and fine for group-size chats — and its output feeds `analyze_group_dynamics`'s top-5 most interactive pairs.

sections.title: Dominant speakers
sections.explanation: `get_dominant_speakers` aggregates message counts per sender, computes each share of the total (rounded to 2 decimals), assigns ranks, and maps the percentage onto an activity ladder — ≥30% Very High, ≥20% High, ≥10% Medium, else Low. An optional `top_n` trims the leaderboard. This is the dominant-speaker detection the tour's Step 10 calls out, and it feeds the engagement summary in the group-dynamics report.

sections.title: summarize_conversation: T5 generation core
sections.explanation: The abstractive core. Empty-frame and no-valid-text guards return honest placeholder dicts rather than feeding garbage to the model. Generation uses the `"summarize: "` input prefix — the comment explains it replaces what the removed `pipeline('summarization')` auto-prepended — tokenizes with `truncation=True, max_length=512`, and calls `model.generate(..., do_sample=False)` for deterministic output, decoding with `skip_special_tokens=True`. Any exception degrades to an `'Error generating summary: ...'` dict so a model hiccup never crashes the pipeline.

sections.title: Date-range and per-participant summaries
sections.explanation: Two filtered wrappers around the core. `summarize_by_date_range` coerces the date column with `errors='coerce'`, applies an inclusive string-comparison mask, and delegates — attaching the `date_range` label; a missing column or empty selection returns a friendly no-messages dict. `summarize_by_participant` filters by sender the same way and attaches the `participant` label. Both keep the contract shape identical to `summarize_conversation`'s result plus one extra key.

sections.title: Periodic summaries and key topics
sections.explanation: `generate_periodic_summaries` groups the chat by pandas Period strings (`'D'`, `'W'`, `'M'`) and summarizes each window with a tighter 50-message cap, returning period bounds plus text. `get_key_topics` is deliberately NOT generative: a `\b[a-zA-Z]{4,}\b` regex tokenization over all messages minus a small stop-word set, then `Counter.most_common(top_n)`. Deterministic, instant, and a useful complement — the model summarizes what happened while frequency counting shows what the chat kept talking about.

sections.title: Full report, group dynamics, quick API
sections.explanation: `generate_full_report` chains everything: an overall summary (150 messages), key topics, and per-participant summaries — and when `max_participants_in_report` is set on a large group, it limits to the top-N senders by message count so a 50-person chat doesn't explode into hundreds of model calls, printing the limitation honestly. `analyze_group_dynamics` bundles group type, speaker statistics, the top-5 interaction pairs, and an engagement summary (most/least active, average messages per person). `quick_summarize` closes the file as the one-line convenience wrapper.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/chart_json.py.overview: Turns the analysis results into interactive ECharts option dictionaries for the single-file HTML report. `build_chart_specs` is the only always-on builder (daily timeline, activity heatmap, participant bars, sentiment, health, 3D network); the gated NLP stage adds the emotion pie and quarterly lines via `build_emotion_spec` / `build_emotion_timeline_spec`. Three design rules shape everything: every builder is individually try/except'd so a failing chart degrades to the report's PNG fallback, every value is coerced to strictly JSON-serializable primitives, and all tooltip formatters are ECharts template strings rather than JS functions that could not survive the JSON pipe.

sections.title: Docstring, imports, shared constants
sections.explanation: The module header states the contract up front: specs are strictly JSON-serializable (numpy scalars converted, NaN dropped/None-converted, dates as ISO strings), every builder never raises, and tooltips use `{b}`/`{d}`-style template strings — a JS function passed through the JSON pipe would arrive as `{}` in the browser. The shared `_DATAZOOM` pairs an inside zoom with a slider so multi-year chats stay navigable, `_LINE_GRID` fixes consistent margins, and `_EMOTION_ORDER`/`_EMOTION_COLORS` pin the six canonical emotions to a fixed matplotlib-tab10 palette so a series' color never depends on data order.

sections.title: build_chart_specs dispatcher
sections.explanation: The single builder entry point the pipeline calls. Six (name, lambda) pairs are iterated with an individual try/except each — a failing builder is logged with `exc_info` and its chart key is simply omitted from the returned dict, which is exactly the signal `write_report` needs to render that chart's base64 PNG fallback instead. Emotion is deliberately absent: the gated NLP stage builds those specs separately so the always-on path stays torch-free.

sections.title: Emotion pie and quarterly specs
sections.explanation: The two NLP-tier chart builders, each returning `None` when its data is missing so the report simply omits the chart div. `build_emotion_spec` tolerates both `distribution` and `emotion_distribution` summary keys and renders a donut pie. `build_emotion_timeline_spec` consumes the precomputed quarterly list — one smooth line per emotion in fixed palette order, yAxis fixed to 0..1, the shared slider dataZoom for long histories, and per-quarter scores coerced through `_float_or_none` so NaN becomes a gap (None) rather than invalid JSON.

sections.title: Daily timeline builder
sections.explanation: `_build_timeline` resamples the canonical frame to daily message counts via `set_index('timestamp').resample('D').size()` and renders a smooth area line. Axis labels are pre-formatted ISO date strings (JSON-safe), rotated 45 degrees with `hideOverlap` for dense ranges, and the shared dataZoom lets users scrub. Early `None` returns when the frame or `timestamp` column is missing keep the builder total.

sections.title: Activity heatmap builder
sections.explanation: The hour × day-of-week heatmap, computed with a plain dict counting loop over `(dayofweek, hour)` pairs. The interesting trick is in the cell data: ECharts heatmap tooltips use the `{b}` name template, so each cell's `name` embeds the full human-readable label — `Mon · 09:00 — 12 msgs` — instead of a formatter function. A `visualMap` scales from the observed maximum through a fixed five-step blue ramp.

sections.title: Participants bar builder
sections.explanation: `_build_participants` renders message counts as a descending horizontal bar chart — horizontal so long sender names fit, with `axisLabel` capped at 110px width and `overflow: 'truncate'` so a pathological name can't blow up the layout. The series styling (fixed blue fill, rounded right corners, `barMaxWidth`) keeps it visually consistent across chats.

sections.title: Sentiment line builder
sections.explanation: Two series: the daily mean of `vader_compound` plus a dashed 7-day rolling average (`min_periods=1` so early days still get a point). The yAxis is pinned to `dataMin`/`dataMax` so a narrow-sentiment chat still uses the full vertical space, and every data point passes through `_float_or_none` — NaN days become `None`, which ECharts renders as a gap instead of crashing on invalid JSON.

sections.title: Health trend line builder
sections.explanation: `_build_health` only builds when the trend frame actually carries a `health_score` column — otherwise it returns `None` and the PNG fallback renders (the D-07 spirit of graceful degradation). The WS-2 note explains the ×100 scaling: scores are 0..1 but the axis is 0..100, matching the matplotlib PNG's rendered span. A dashed red `markLine` at 50 gives the visual midline reference.

sections.title: True 3D network builder
sections.explanation: The report's showpiece, and the reason the echarts-gl bundle is vendored: a TRUE 3D layout via `nx.spring_layout(graph, dim=3, seed=42)`, centered and normalized to roughly [-50, 50] to match the `grid3D` box. Node `value` packs `[x, y, z, degree]` and a hidden `visualMap` maps degree to symbol size (8..28) and a green ramp; each edge is a `lines3D` segment with opacity scaled by its weight relative to the maximum. `viewControl` enables perspective auto-rotate with drag/zoom sensitivity — the drag-to-rotate interaction the tour highlights. Under 2 nodes (or on any failure) the builder returns `None` and the PNG renders instead.

sections.title: JSON-safety coercion helper
sections.explanation: `_float_or_none` is the tiny function that underwrites the module's serializability rule: coerce to `float`, mapping NaN/None/type errors to `None`, because NaN is never a valid JSON number and would otherwise produce broken JavaScript in the inlined `CHART_SPECS`. Every line-series data path in this module routes values through it.

src/chat_analyzer/cli/report_html.py.overview: Renders the project's deliverable: one self-contained, offline HTML report. A Jinja2 autoescape template (an inline constant, no external assets or CDN) combines the `AnalysisResults` payload with two interactive layers — chart PNG data URIs validated at the boundary, and JSON-serialized ECharts specs rendered by the inlined, license-shipped ECharts bundles. Chat content is treated as UNTRUSTED: autoescape is set explicitly, chart URIs must match the internal `data:image/png;base64` prefix, specs must be JSON-serializable dicts, and all inlined JavaScript is scrubbed of `</script` and `<!--`. The report is always generated, written UTF-8 to a sanitized filename in the cwd, and best-effort auto-opened.

sections.title: Docstring, imports, boundary constants
sections.explanation: The header states the security posture plainly: jinja2's autoescape defaults to False, so it is set explicitly because chat content is untrusted input, and chart URIs are validated before they ever reach the template. The three constants define the boundaries used later: `_INVALID_FILENAME_CHARS` strips Windows-invalid and control characters, `_CHART_PREFIX` is the only accepted PNG data-URI scheme, and `_CHART_KEYS` lists the eight chart slots in template order — a spec key missing from the JSON renders that chart's PNG fallback instead.

sections.title: Inline-JS scrubbing and vendored assets
sections.explanation: `_inline_js` neutralizes the two strings that could break an inline `<script>`: `</script` (which would close the element early) and `<!--` (which could open comment mode in old parsers). It is applied to ALL inlined JS — both vendored ECharts bundles and the report runtime — and combined with the template's `|tojson` escaping it means even a `</script>` payload inside a participant name cannot survive into the report. `_load_inline_asset` reads the bundles from package assets via `importlib.resources` (working for both editable and wheel installs) and degrades to an empty string when missing, so the report still renders with PNG charts rather than crashing.

sections.title: Report runtime JS
sections.explanation: The browser runtime, kept as a scrubbed module constant in deliberately plain ES5. `webglAvailable()` feature-detects WebGL and `fallbackNetwork()` swaps the 3D network div for its hidden PNG twin. `initCharts` loops the eight known keys, instantiating `echarts.init` only for divs that exist with a non-empty spec series — skipping the network entirely without WebGL — and adds a sentiment-specific numeric tooltip formatter. `showTab` toggles panel/button classes and triggers `resizeVisibleCharts` on the next animation frame, because ECharts canvases sized while hidden come up wrong.

sections.title: Template shell: styles, header, tabs
sections.explanation: The template opens with all CSS inline (part of the single-file guarantee) and a header showing title/subtitle. Two honest-reporting touches appear early: a conditional `skip-note` renders whenever `parse.skipped_lines > 0`, surfacing the parser's honest skip counting, and the nav builds the nine tab buttons — overview, participants, flow, words, sentiment, health, network, emotion, and the narrative tab labeled 'What's going on'.

sections.title: Overview to sentiment panels
sections.explanation: Each panel pairs a narrative 'lead' insight (indexed out of `results['insights']`) with its chart slot and stats table. The repeated `{% if charts_json.NAME %}...{% else %}{% if charts.NAME %}` idiom is the interactive-vs-PNG switch: when an ECharts spec exists, an empty div is rendered for the runtime to hydrate; otherwise the base64 PNG `` shows. This block covers overview (totals table), participants (per-person counts/lengths/shares), flow (busiest day, peak hour, avg response time), words (top words and emojis), and sentiment (distribution table plus the score legend).

sections.title: Health and network panels
sections.explanation: The health panel shows overall score, grade, initiator balance, and average response minutes. The network panel adds an explanatory meta-line about edge-weight semantics (consecutive-sender turn exchanges) and a special structure: when BOTH the interactive spec and the PNG exist, the `` is rendered hidden alongside the div so the runtime's `fallbackNetwork` can reveal it if WebGL is missing or `echarts.init` throws. The table reports node/edge counts, density, and the strongest-connection summary.

sections.title: Emotion and narrative panels
sections.explanation: Emotion is the tier-gated panel: when the NLP stage didn't run, it renders an honest install hint (`pip install chat-analyzer-pro[nlp]`) instead of charts; when it ran in sampled mode, it labels results 'based on a sample of N of M messages' next to both the quarterly chart and the overall distribution — the sampled-path honesty from Step 10 made visible. The narrative panel renders the Tier A/B lead, the optional generative summary, and the hedged observations with their confidence tags.

sections.title: Script injection and CHART_SPECS
sections.explanation: The closing script block assembles the interactive runtime in a deliberate order: the two vendored bundles first (inlined with `|safe` — they are trusted, scrubbed constants, and autoescape would otherwise corrupt operators like `<` inside the JS), then `CHART_SPECS` built with `|tojson` for each of the eight slots, then the report runtime whose `DOMContentLoaded` listener initializes the charts. This ordering is what makes the offline report interactive with zero network access.

sections.title: Boundary validation helpers
sections.explanation: Three guards that keep untrusted or malformed data out of the template. `sanitize_filename` strips path separators, Windows-invalid and control characters, leading dots/whitespace, and falls back to `chat_analysis` when nothing survives. `_json_serializable` round-trips `json.dumps(value, allow_nan=False)` — rejecting numpy scalars, NaN, and arbitrary objects. `_validate_charts_json` keeps only dict-shaped, serializable specs for the eight known keys, substituting `{}` for anything else so the template's falsy check falls back to that chart's PNG.

sections.title: write_report and open_report
sections.explanation: `write_report` is the final assembly point. It validates chart URIs at the boundary (only internally generated `data:image/png;base64` strings pass), validates the interactive specs, and derives the narrative lead from the tier status — 'Tier B enabled (local generative model)' versus 'Tier A (statistical inference, speculative)'. Rendering uses an explicitly-autoescaping Environment; the file is written with `encoding='utf-8'` (the Pitfall 11 note: never the platform default, or emoji chats corrupt on Windows cp1252) to a sanitized `<stem>_report.html` in the CWD — not the input directory (D-09). `open_report` honors the `CHAT_ANALYZER_NO_OPEN=1` opt-out and degrades to a logged False rather than ever crashing.

src/chat_analyzer/assets/LICENSE.echarts.overview: The full Apache License 2.0 text that ships with the vendored Apache ECharts bundle (`echarts.min.js`) inlined into every generated report. Because the minified library is redistributed inside the wheel and embedded in user-facing HTML, the license text must travel with it — this file plus the appended subcomponent notice is what keeps the offline single-file report legally clean.

sections.title: Apache 2.0 terms and ECharts notice
sections.explanation: The complete Apache License 2.0: §2–3 grant a perpetual, royalty-free copyright AND patent license (with the clause terminating patent grants for litigation filers), §4 sets the redistribution conditions — pass the license along, carry change notices, retain attribution, and reproduce NOTICE contents — followed by the trademark clause, warranty disclaimer, and liability limits. The appended ECharts-specific appendix (lines 208–222) declares that the Apache ECharts project itself embeds d3.js under BSD 3-Clause in four source files (treemap layout, tree layoutHelper, graph forceHelper, number util), so downstream users inherit that notice too. Shipping this copy inside `src/chat_analyzer/assets/` satisfies §4's requirement while the bundle is vendored and inlined offline.

src/chat_analyzer/assets/LICENSE.echarts.overview: The BSD 3-Clause license for the vendored `echarts-gl` build (Copyright (c) 2017, Baidu Inc.) — the WebGL extension that powers the report's drag-to-rotate 3D network view. Like the ECharts license beside it, it ships in `assets/` because the minified bundle is vendored into the wheel and inlined into every generated HTML report.

sections.title: BSD 3-Clause for echarts-gl
sections.explanation: The standard three-clause BSD text: redistribution in source or binary form is permitted provided the copyright notice is retained in source, reproduced in documentation for binary distributions, and the copyright holder's name is never used to endorse derived products without permission — closed out by the AS-IS warranty disclaimer and liability limitation. This is the permissive license that makes it trivial to vendor the GL build responsible for `scatter3D`/`lines3D` on `grid3D` and the auto-rotating `viewControl` in `chart_json._build_network`.

tests/golden/whatsapp_sample.csv.overview: One half of the golden-parity regression baseline: a long-format `metric,value` CSV holding the expected aggregate stats for the bundled WhatsApp sample fixture, captured from a real tier-1 pipeline run (`nlp_enabled=False` — no torch, no transformers). `tests/test_golden_parity.py` re-runs the live pipeline on the same fixture and asserts this exact projection matches, so a fresh clone verifies the whole parse → DataFrame → EDA → VADER path in seconds. The headline numbers — 27 parsed messages from 2 participants over 2023-12-25..27 with `avg_compound` 0.503544 — are what CI protects.

sections.title: Header: long-format metric,value
sections.explanation: A single header row defines the format the parity harness parses with `line.partition(',')`: a metric name in contract-path notation (`stats.media_messages`) and a string value. The long, one-metric-per-row layout is what makes the golden stable under contract drift — the test's exact key-set assert trips FIRST on any added/renamed/removed metric, before any value is compared.

sections.title: Locked metrics: parse, stats, sentiment
sections.explanation: Nine locked values mirroring the `AnalysisResults` projection: the parse block (27 parsed, 0 skipped, 0 system messages), the stats block (2 media messages from the `<Media omitted>` markers, 27 total, 2 participants, date range 2023-12-25 to 2023-12-27), and `sentiment.avg_compound = 0.503544` — the mean VADER compound the adapter exposes. Only `avg_compound` is a float: the harness compares it with `pytest.approx(rel=1e-4, abs=1e-6)` because the golden rounds to 6 decimals, while every int/string here compares exactly.

tests/golden/telegram_sample.csv.overview: The Telegram half of the golden-parity baseline: expected aggregates for the bundled `telegram_sample.json` fixture (a 5-message bare-Chat export), captured from a real tier-1 run. Same long format and same nine-metric projection contract as the WhatsApp golden — `tests/test_golden_parity.py` consumes both in one parametrized pattern. Notable shape: 3 participants conversing within a single day, zero media, and a milder average VADER compound of 0.291540.

sections.title: Header: long-format metric,value
sections.explanation: Identical header contract to the WhatsApp golden: metric names on the left, string values on the right, parsed line-by-line with `partition(',')`. Keeping both goldens in the same format lets `_read_golden` and the key-set comparison work unchanged across fixtures.

sections.title: Locked metrics: parse, stats, sentiment
sections.explanation: The Telegram projection: parse counters 5/0/0 (parsed/skipped/system), stats with 0 media messages, 5 total messages, 3 participants, and a single-day date range (2025-09-15 to 2025-09-15) — a deliberately tiny group-chat fixture that exercises the multi-participant path. `sentiment.avg_compound = 0.291540` is the lone float, compared with `pytest.approx` tolerances; all other values match exactly.

tests/test_golden_parity.py.overview: The clone-friendly regression gate that makes the optimization claims from Steps 8–9 checkable: it re-runs the REAL pipeline (`nlp_enabled=False`, tier-1) on the two committed sample fixtures and asserts a nine-metric projection matches the golden CSVs in `tests/golden/`. No NLP models are needed, so a fresh clone verifies the entire parse → DataFrame → EDA → VADER path in seconds. The projection deliberately mirrors the `AnalysisResults` contract shape, so a rename anywhere in that contract fails the exact key-set assert first — before any value comparison.

sections.title: Harness design rationale
sections.explanation: The docstring lays out the whole strategy: goldens were captured on the author machine by running the real pipeline with `nlp_enabled=False` (no torch, no transformers), the test re-runs that same pipeline on the committed fixtures, and float metrics compare with `pytest.approx(rel=1e-4, abs=1e-6)` because the goldens round to 6 decimal places while ints/strings compare exactly. The last sentence is the design's teeth: the metric-key set must match the golden exactly, so a contract rename (the example given is moving `media_messages` out of `stats`) trips the key assert first.

sections.title: Paths, float set, fixture mapping
sections.explanation: Small setup with one important detail: `DATA` and `GOLDEN_DIR` are resolved relative to `__file__`, so the harness works from any working directory. `FLOAT_METRICS` names the only float-compared metric (`sentiment.avg_compound`); everything else in the golden is an exact int or string. `FIXTURES` pairs each golden CSV with its input file, mapping `whatsapp_sample.csv` → the `.txt` export and `telegram_sample.csv` → the `.json` export.

sections.title: Metric projection from AnalysisResults
sections.explanation: `_console` builds a quiet rich `Console` writing to a `StringIO` with `force_terminal=False`, so `run_pipeline`'s stage narration never pollutes test output. `project` then extracts the nine stable metrics from the nested results dict — the parse counters, the stats block scalars, the date-range start/end, and the sentiment block's `avg_compound`. The inline comment documents a real contract subtlety: `media_messages` lives under `stats` (the adapter computes `max(marker count, zip file count)`), NOT in the parse block, despite sitting next to parse counters in the golden.

sections.title: Golden CSV reader
sections.explanation: `_read_golden` is the long-format counterpart of the projection: skip the header row, partition each remaining line on the first comma, strip both sides, and skip blank lines. Values stay strings until comparison time, which is why the float branch of the assertion does its own `float()` conversion.

sections.title: Parity assertion with key-set gate
sections.explanation: `_assert_parity` runs `run_pipeline` live on the fixture, projects the results, and reads the golden — then asserts `set(projected) == set(golden)` BEFORE any value comparison, making contract drift fail structurally with a message that shows both sorted key lists. The value loop then branches: float metrics must not be None (they must never be on a parsed chat) and compare through `pytest.approx`, while everything else compares `str(live) == expected` exactly. This ordering — shape first, values second — is the harness's core design.

sections.title: The two fixture tests
sections.explanation: Two thin pytest functions calling `_assert_parity` for the WhatsApp text export and the Telegram JSON export respectively. Because both fixtures are committed and the tier-1 path needs no downloads, the lean CI job (Step 13's `test` job) exercises the whole always-on pipeline — parsing, canonical DataFrame, EDA, VADER scoring, adapter projection — on every push in seconds.

.github/workflows/ci.yml.overview: The GitHub Actions quality gate protecting the tiered architecture from Step 1 onward. Three parallel jobs split the suite the way docs/TESTING.md describes: a lean matrix (ubuntu/windows × Python 3.11/3.12) running only the fast suite with a branch-coverage floor, a slow job exercising the wall-clock CLI/e2e tests plus the single ruff lint pass, and an NLP job proving the optional `[nlp]` extra actually installs. A concurrency group cancels superseded in-progress runs on the same ref so a newer push wins.

sections.title: Triggers and concurrency
sections.explanation: The workflow runs on every `push` and `pull_request` to any branch — no path filters, matching the repo's treat-every-commit-seriously stance. The `concurrency` block groups runs by `workflow + ref` with `cancel-in-progress: true`, the standard GitHub Actions idiom for abandoning superseded runs on the same branch so queued CI doesn't pile up during rapid pushes.

sections.title: Lean matrix job (test)
sections.explanation: The primary gate: `fail-fast: false` over a 2×2 matrix (ubuntu-latest/windows-latest × Python 3.11/3.12) so one platform's failure doesn't mask the others. All three jobs share the same env hygiene — `BROWSER=__none__`, `CHAT_ANALYZER_NO_OPEN=1`, `CHAT_ANALYZER_FORCE_NLP=0` — to suppress browser spawning and NLP forcing in CI. After `pip install -e '.[dev]'`, it runs `pytest -m 'not slow'` with `--cov=chat_analyzer --cov-branch --cov-fail-under=50`: the coverage floor exists to catch mass test deletion or broken collection (TEST-02), set at 50 with headroom below the measured ~59% branch coverage.

sections.title: Slow job plus ruff lint
sections.explanation: A single ubuntu/3.11 job for everything wall-clock-heavy that the matrix shouldn't pay for four times: the `slow`-marked CLI subprocess spawns and full pipeline/report renders. It also runs `ruff check src tests` once here — linting executes a single time rather than per matrix combination, a deliberate cost trade. No torch is needed; the slow suite is a base-install suite.

sections.title: NLP extra verification job
sections.explanation: The job that proves Step 3's optional-extra design actually works: `pip install -e '.[dev,nlp]'` pulls in the heavy torch/transformers dependencies, and the fact that the install succeeds is itself part of the assertion. It then runs `tests/test_phase4_nlp.py` specifically — the file whose gate-ON cases skip when transformers is absent, so with the extra installed they exercise the real model-load mock path end to end. This keeps the `[nlp]` dependency set from silently rotting.

docs/TESTING.md.overview: The suite's map: 330 tests across 31 files (304 fast plus 26 wall-clock-slow), what each area covers, the conventions every new test must follow, and how the suite splits across the three CI jobs. It operationalizes the tour's testing themes — the `slow` marker, D-17's rule that the fast suite never touches the network, real-modules-not-copies, and the golden-parity harness. Reading it alongside `ci.yml` (Step 13) closes the loop on how the tiered, parity-tested architecture stays honest.

sections.title: Suite shape and philosophy
sections.explanation: Opens with the inventory — 330 tests, 31 files, 304 fast + 26 slow — and the mechanism: the `slow` marker is registered in pyproject's `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`, no `addopts` are set, and fast-only is an explicit `-m "not slow"`. The philosophy paragraph is the important part: tests exercise the REAL shipped modules, mocking only heavyweight external callables (transformers pipelines, T5 loads, `webbrowser`) and shaping the mocks to return exactly what the real libraries return. Real-model inference happens in exactly one place — the slow-marked emotion spawn-parity smoke — enforcing D-17.

sections.title: Framework and setup
sections.explanation: Practical setup rules: the package must be installed before tests run (the `src/` layout means tests import `from chat_analyzer...`), and the install command is `pip install -e ".[dev]"` — extended to `.[dev,nlp]` only for NLP-gated tests, which skip cleanly when transformers is absent. It also flags the four legacy files that still use `unittest.TestCase` classes with `__main__` runners; pytest collects them normally, and new tests are plain pytest functions.

sections.title: Command matrix
sections.explanation: A verified command table: full suite, fast-only (the CI default), slow-only, single file, single function, and `-k` keyword selection — plus the ruff gate CI runs.
